W1: Welcome Back: Simple & Continuous Review

Weekly plan ·

Required lesson and practice

Four tenses, one bus ride

Scene  Tuesday, 5:15 PM. Rosa waits for the 116 to class. Photo: Osman Rana / Unsplash

Welcome back! Catch up with Rosa and David. Read for the message first.

🧑🏽
David
Hey, Rosa! Ready to be back?
👩🏾
Rosa
Almost! Last night I was doing the dishes when my daughter asked, ‘Mom, where are my gym shoes?’
🧑🏽
David
First-day chaos?
👩🏾
Rosa
Totally! We leave everything by the door on school nights. But last night? One shoe was still under the couch.
🧑🏽
David
That sounds like my house. How’s today going?
👩🏾
Rosa
Better. My sister is helping with my daughter this week. Now I just need to find MY notebook!

Time words give clues. Think about the situation.

These names help us talk about corrections. You don’t need to name the tense before speaking.

  • Present simple: a routine or stable fact. “We leave everything by the door on school nights.”
  • Present continuous: happening now or temporarily. “My sister is helping with my daughter this week.”
  • Past simple: a completed past event. “My daughter asked about her gym shoes.”
  • Past continuous: in progress at a past moment. “I was doing the dishes.”

What is Rosa telling David?

Choose the meaning that fits their conversation.

  1. Why is today easier for Rosa?

    The children don’t have school. / Her sister is helping with her daughter this week. / She found her notebook.

    Answer / teacher checktemporary
  2. What was Rosa doing when her daughter asked about the gym shoes?

    Rosa was doing the dishes. / Rosa was riding the bus. / Rosa was working at the clinic.

    Answer / teacher checkkids

Your usual routine · Present Simple

Scene  East Boston. Tuesday evening after work. Photo: CDMA / Unsplash
🧑🏽
Classmate
You always have food in that bag!
👩🏾
Rosa
Of course. My daughter gets hungry the minute we leave the house.
🧑🏽
Classmate
Same with my son. He says, ‘I’m not hungry.’ Then he eats my sandwich.
👩🏾
Rosa
Exactly! I pack two sandwiches now. One for her and one for me.

Rosa and her classmate know this routine well. What do you always carry in your bag?

Quick form check: I/you/we/they work; he/she/it works.

Timeline labels: (present)

Tell someone about the routine

Choose or type the form that fits. For a blank, type only the missing word.

  1. Rosa says, “I pack two sandwiches every day. My daughter eat one on the bus.” Fix the second sentence.

    My daughter eat one on the bus. / My daughter eating one on the bus. / My daughter eats one on the bus.

    Answer / teacher checkeats
  2. “My son always ___ for a snack as soon as we get on the bus.” (ask)
    Answer / teacher checkasks
  3. “We ___ two sandwiches every morning. One is never enough!” (pack)
    Answer / teacher checkpack

What’s happening now? · Present Continuous

Scene  Before class, Rosa gets a message from her sister Teresa. Photo: Ivan Aleksic / Unsplash
👩‍👧
Teresa
Quick question. Where’s the rice?
👩🏾
Rosa
Top shelf, next to the pasta. What are you making?
👩‍👧
Teresa
I’m making dinner. Your daughter is helping me. Well, she’s eating some pineapple.
👩🏾
Rosa
Ha! Save some for me. I’m hungry already.

Rosa’s sister is making dinner while Rosa waits for class. What’s happening at your home right now?

Quick form check: use am/is/are + verb-ing: “I’m making dinner.”

Timeline labels: (present)

Give an update

Think about what is happening. For a blank, type only the missing words.

  1. Rosa’s sister sends a photo from the kitchen: “Your daughter ___ all the pineapple!” (eat)
    Answer / teacher checkis eating
  2. Rosa’s sister usually works evenings. This week she’s off. Which message tells Rosa about her help just for this week?

    I make dinner for your daughter every week. / I’m making dinner for your daughter this week. / I made dinner for your daughter last week.

    Answer / teacher checktemporary
  3. Her sister texts: “We’re in the kitchen. We ___ dinner now. Come hungry!” (make)
    Answer / teacher checkare making

Tell a past story · Past Simple and Continuous

Scene  First day of school. Two different shoes. Photo: Franck V. / Unsplash
👩‍🏫
Ms. Tran
How was the first day of school for your kids? Everyone on time?
🙋🏽‍♂️
Hector
Almost. We were waiting for the bus when my son looked down at his feet.
👩‍🏫
Ms. Tran
Uh-oh. What was wrong?
🙋🏽‍♂️
Hector
One red sneaker, one yellow sneaker! He was putting them on in the dark when I called him.
👩‍🏫
Ms. Tran
Oh no! Did you go back home?
🙋🏽‍♂️
Hector
No time. The bus came. After school, I found his other red one in the dog’s bed!

They were already waiting for the bus when the boy noticed his shoes. There was no time to go home, so he wore them to school.

Quick form check: past simple uses a past form, such as looked or found. Past continuous uses was/were + verb-ing.

“Yesterday” can go with either tense: “Yesterday I cooked dinner.” “Yesterday at six, I was cooking dinner.” The speaker’s meaning matters.

Timeline labels: (past) → (past)

Two different sneakers

Complete the story. Type only the missing words.

  1. The bus wasn’t there yet. “We ___ at the stop when my son noticed his shoes.” (wait)
    Answer / teacher checkwere waiting
  2. “After school, I ___ his other red sneaker in the dog’s bed.” (find)
    Answer / teacher checkfound
  3. “It was still dark this morning. My son ___ on his sneakers when I called him.” (put)
    Answer / teacher checkwas putting

Your turn: catch up, check, try again

First, try it with support. Say the replies aloud or write them in your notebook. Use your own details.

🧑🏽
Classmate
What’s one thing you always do before you leave home?
🙋
You
I usually …
🧑🏽
Classmate
Anything different at home or work this week?
🙋
You
This week, I am …
🧑🏽
Classmate
Any surprises this week? Something you forgot, a funny moment, or a change of plans?
🙋
You
I was … when …

Now make it yours. Look away from the starters. Catch up with a partner, speak aloud to yourself, or write a short message: share your routine, something temporary, and a past story. You can invent details.

Say it → check one sentence → say it again.

“I doing the dishes when my daughter asked about her gym shoes.”

I mean the dishes were not finished yet. Past continuous needs was/were.

“I was doing the dishes when my daughter asked about her gym shoes.”

Choose just one sentence from your catch-up. Does it express your meaning? Use the tense reference if you need help checking the verb. Then say or write the sentence again. If it already works, keep it!

Guide mini-quiz

  1. “Why do you always bring two sandwiches?” Which answer explains Rosa’s routine?

    I’m packing a sandwich for my sister today. / My daughter eats one of them on the bus. / I forgot my lunch yesterday.

    AnswerMy daughter eats one of them on the bus.

    Present simple describes what usually happens: ‘My daughter eats one of them.’

  2. Rosa’s sister sends a photo of dinner cooking on the stove: “I ___ rice. Do you want some?” (cook)
    Answeram cooking

    Present continuous describes what is happening now: ‘I’m cooking rice.’ I’m means I am.

  3. “We couldn’t find her gym shoe. Then my daughter ___ under the couch and found it.” (look)

    looked / look / looking

    Answerlooked

    Past simple tells what happened next: ‘My daughter looked under the couch.’

  4. ‘I was doing the dishes when my daughter asked about her gym shoes.’ What was happening?

    Rosa started the dishes after her daughter asked. / Rosa had already finished the dishes. / Rosa was still doing the dishes when her daughter spoke.

    AnswerRosa was still doing the dishes when her daughter spoke.

    Past continuous (‘was doing’) shows what Rosa was in the middle of. Past simple (‘asked’) tells what happened during it.

  5. Repair this past story: "I looking for my keys when the bus arrived."

    I am looking for my keys when the bus arrived. / I was looking for my keys when the bus arrived. / I were looking for my keys when the bus arrived.

    AnswerI was looking for my keys when the bus arrived.

    Past continuous needs was/were + verb-ing. With I, use was. Say the repaired sentence again: ‘I was looking for my keys when the bus arrived.’

W2: Parts of Speech Guide

Weekly plan ·

Required lesson and practice

Nouns: naming the world around you

Scene  East Boston Community Center. Tuesday, 5:30 PM. Amara writes down her information. Photo: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash

Amara cleans patient rooms at a hospital. She works days and has two kids, so she can only study at night. Today she comes straight from work to sign up for a free English class. James works at the front desk.

🙋🏼
James
Hi. This is the registration desk. Can I get your name and address?
👩🏾
Amara
Amara Yusuf. My address is 24 Meridian Street, near the hospital.
🙋🏼
James
Thanks. Please fill out this form. You will also need a pencil and a notebook for class.
👩🏾
Amara
I have a notebook in my bag. Could I borrow a pencil?

Look at the words in bold: desk, name, address, street, hospital, form, pencil, notebook, bag. Each one is a name for a place or a thing. These words are nouns.

Nouns name people, places, things, and ideas. If you can say "a ___" or "the ___" in front of it, it is probably a noun.

person a volunteer, the teacher, Amara, a student
place the community center, Meridian Street, the second floor
thing a pencil, a notebook, the form, a bag
idea English, education, registration, progress

Thing or idea?

A thing is something you can touch: a pencil, a notebook, the form, a bag.

An idea is something you cannot touch. You can only think about it or feel it: English, education, registration, progress.

Ask yourself: can I pick it up with my hands? If no, it is an idea.

Singular and plural:

one class / two classes

a student / many students

Most nouns add -s or -es to become plural.

Spot the noun

Choose the noun in each sentence.

  1. Amara fills out a form at the community center.

    fills / form / out

    Answer / teacher checkform
  2. The volunteer explains each question carefully.

    explains / carefully / volunteer

    Answer / teacher checkvolunteer
  3. She carries a pencil and a notebook in her bag.

    carries / pencil / in

    Answer / teacher checkpencil

Person, place, thing, or idea?

What kind of noun is it? Remember: a thing is something you can touch. An idea is something you cannot touch.

  1. What kind of noun is the word 'hospital'?

    Person (who) / Place (where) / Thing (you can touch it) / Idea (you cannot touch it)

    Answer / teacher checkplace
  2. What kind of noun is the word 'education'?

    Person (who) / Place (where) / Thing (you can touch it) / Idea (you cannot touch it)

    Answer / teacher checkidea
  3. What kind of noun is the word 'notebook'?

    Person (who) / Place (where) / Thing (you can touch it) / Idea (you cannot touch it)

    Answer / teacher checkthing

Build the sentence

Put the words in the correct order.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkThe volunteer hands Amara a form
  2. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkThe supply closet is behind the first door

Singular or plural?

Write the plural form of the noun.

  1. one notebook / two ___
    Answer / teacher checknotebooks
  2. one box / three ___
    Answer / teacher checkboxes

Verbs: action verbs and state verbs

Samuel fixes things in Amara's building, and he volunteers at the center on Tuesdays. He helps Amara with her registration form. Look at what each of them does, and what is true about each of them.

Sort
Action verbs and state verbs
Action State
Samuel helps, fixes knows, understands
Amara fills out, writes wants, needs, has, knows

The words in bold in the table are verbs. But they are not all the same kind. Some are things you do. Some are things that are true about you.

There are two types of verbs. Action verbs describe things you do. State verbs describe things that are true about you, such as what you feel, know, have, or think.

Action verbs: things you do

action Samuel helps students every Tuesday. He explains the schedule.
action Amara fills out the form. She writes her address in the first box.

State verbs: things that are true

state Amara knows Samuel from her building. She remembers his face.
state She wants the evening class. She understands why it is a good fit.
state Amara has two children. She needs a class in the evening.

Why does this matter?

State verbs are almost never used in the continuous (-ing) form.

✗ I am knowing the answer.

✓ I know the answer.

Common state verbs: know, want, need, understand, remember, believe, like, love, hate, have, seem.

Can you do it right now?: Ask yourself: can I watch someone do this? If yes, it is probably an action verb (run, write, help). If no, it is probably a state verb (know, want, understand). You cannot watch someone 'know' something.

Action or state?

Choose the correct label for the verb in bold.

  1. Samuel <strong>helps</strong> new students every Tuesday.

    Action verb: you can watch someone do it / State verb: a feeling, a fact, or something in the mind

    Answer / teacher checkaction
  2. Amara <strong>knows</strong> Samuel from her building.

    Action verb: you can watch someone do it / State verb: a feeling, a fact, or something in the mind

    Answer / teacher checkstate
  3. She <strong>fills out</strong> the form at the registration desk.

    Action verb: you can watch someone do it / State verb: a feeling, a fact, or something in the mind

    Answer / teacher checkaction
  4. Amara <strong>wants</strong> an evening class.

    Action verb: you can watch someone do it / State verb: a feeling, a fact, or something in the mind

    Answer / teacher checkstate

Correct or not?

State verbs do not use the -ing form. Is each sentence correct?

  1. "I am knowing all the students in my class."

    Correct: this verb can use the -ing form. / Not correct: this verb cannot use the -ing form.

    Answer / teacher checkincorrect
  2. "Samuel is helping a student right now."

    Correct: this verb can use the -ing form. / Not correct: this verb cannot use the -ing form.

    Answer / teacher checkcorrect
  3. "She is wanting the evening class."

    Correct: this verb can use the -ing form. / Not correct: this verb cannot use the -ing form.

    Answer / teacher checkincorrect

Read the table

Look at the table about Samuel and Amara.

  1. Look at the table. Which verb is an action verb for Amara?

    needs / has / fills out

    Answer / teacher checkfills out
  2. Look at the table. How many state verbs does Amara have in her row? Write a number.
    Answer / teacher check4,four

Fill in the verb

Write the correct form of the verb in parentheses.

  1. Amara ___ the evening class. (want)
    Answer / teacher checkwants
  2. Samuel ___ new students find the right class. (help)
    Answer / teacher checkhelps

Build the sentence

Unscramble the words.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkSamuel helps new students every Tuesday
  2. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkAmara sees Samuel at the coffee shop

Adjectives: describing words

Dilnoza sits down next to Amara. She is a cashier at a supermarket, and she is signing up for the same class. The last part of the form is called "About You." Names of things are not enough here. They need to describe their lives. First, Dilnoza reads about a real person who moved to a new country. Look at the words that describe.

Famous person
Hamdi Ulukaya: A New Country

Hamdi Ulukaya grew up on a mountain in eastern Turkey, near the Euphrates River. Later, he moved to the United States, a new country. In 2005, he started Chobani, a yogurt company.

In 2016, he started Tent. Tent helps large businesses hire refugees. Today, it works with more than 500 of the world's largest employers. Ulukaya says, "The minute a refugee gets a job is the minute they stop being a refugee."

Photo: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, public domain. Sources: Tent: Hamdi Ulukaya, Tent: About

Adjectives describe nouns. They answer what kind? or how many? Adjectives usually come right before the noun they describe.

what kind Amara has a full-time job. She works in a busy hospital.
what kind They live in a new building on a quiet street.
how many Amara has two children. Dilnoza has three brothers.
how many The form has five sections. The first section asks for your name.

Adjective position:

a small apartment (adjective before noun)

The apartment is small. (adjective after is/are/was)

Find the adjective

Choose the adjective in each sentence.

  1. Amara has a full-time job at a busy hospital.

    job / busy / has

    Answer / teacher checkbusy
  2. Dilnoza lives in a small apartment with her sister.

    lives / apartment / small

    Answer / teacher checksmall
  3. Dilnoza has three brothers.

    has / three / brothers

    Answer / teacher checkthree

Read about Hamdi Ulukaya

Look at the reading.

  1. Look at the reading. Where did Hamdi Ulukaya grow up?

    In the United States / In eastern Turkey / In a city on the coast

    Answer / teacher checkeastern
  2. Look at the reading. In what year did he start Tent? Write the year.
    Answer / teacher check2016
  3. Look at the reading. Which word describes the noun "country"?

    started / later / new

    Answer / teacher checknew

Correct or not?

Is the adjective in the right place?

  1. "She has a schedule busy."

    Correct: the adjective is in the right place. / Not correct: the adjective is in the wrong place.

    Answer / teacher checkincorrect
  2. "The new building has two small rooms."

    Correct: the adjective is in the right place. / Not correct: the adjective is in the wrong place.

    Answer / teacher checkcorrect
  3. "They have children three."

    Correct: the adjective is in the right place. / Not correct: the adjective is in the wrong place.

    Answer / teacher checkincorrect

Build the sentence

Unscramble the words to make a correct sentence.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkDilnoza has a busy schedule this week
  2. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkThe form has five short sections

Write the adjective

Write the word that describes the noun.

  1. "Dilnoza has a busy schedule." Which word describes "schedule"?
    Answer / teacher checkbusy
  2. "The new building has two small rooms." Which word describes "rooms"?
    Answer / teacher checksmall

Adverbs: how, when, how often

On Saturday, it's cleanup day at Amara's building. Samuel is outside in work gloves, writing repairs on a clipboard. Amara tells him her kitchen sink is leaking again. Then she asks how his week works. This is what he tells her.

Chart
Samuel's week: how often?
always
100% Samuel always helps at the center on Tuesdays.
usually
80% He usually fixes a leak in one visit.
sometimes
40% He sometimes eats lunch at his desk.
rarely
10% He rarely takes a day off.
never
0% He never leaves a job unfinished.

"I can fix the sink on Monday," he says, and writes it down. Words like always tell us how often. Other words tell us when and how. They are all adverbs.

Adverbs describe verbs. They answer how?, when?, or how often? Many adverbs end in -ly (quickly, carefully, quietly). But not all of them do (well, hard, early, fast). A group of words can do the same job: every Tuesday, last year, after work.

how Samuel works quickly. He speaks English well.
when He finishes early. He comes after his shift on Tuesdays.
how often He volunteers every week. He always arrives on time.

Adjective or adverb? The question is: what does it describe?

Adjective Samuel is a quick worker. (describes the noun "worker")
Adverb Samuel works quickly. (describes the verb "works")
Adjective His English is good. (describes the noun "English")
Adverb He speaks English well. (describes the verb "speaks")

Careful: hard and hardly

Samuel works hard. (with a lot of effort)

Samuel hardly works. (almost never, the opposite meaning)

Adding -ly does not always make the adverb. Hardly is a different word with a different meaning.

good vs. well: Good is an adjective: his English is good. Well is an adverb: he speaks English well. This pair catches many learners, including native speakers.

Adjective or adverb?

Choose the correct word for each sentence.

  1. Samuel is a ___ worker. He fixes most things the same day. (quick / quickly)

    quick (adjective) / quickly (adverb)

    Answer / teacher checkquick
  2. He finishes his work very ___. He is always done before noon. (quick / quickly)

    quick (adjective) / quickly (adverb)

    Answer / teacher checkquickly
  3. Dilnoza speaks English ___. She practices every day. (good / well)

    good (adjective) / well (adverb)

    Answer / teacher checkwell
  4. Her pronunciation is ___. People understand her easily. (good / well)

    good (adjective) / well (adverb)

    Answer / teacher checkgood

Read the chart

Look at Samuel's chart.

  1. Look at Samuel's chart. Which sentence is true?

    Samuel never takes a day off. / Samuel rarely takes a day off. / Samuel always takes a day off.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  2. Look at Samuel's chart. He ___ eats lunch at his desk. (Write one word.)
    Answer / teacher checksometimes

Fill in the adverb

Write the adverb form of the word in parentheses.

  1. Samuel explains the form ___. Everyone understands. (clear)
    Answer / teacher checkclearly
  2. Amara listens ___ during the orientation. (careful)
    Answer / teacher checkcarefully

All four working together

Scene  Tuesday, 6:20 PM. The board by the door at the community center, full of flyers and notices. Photo: Zoshua Colah / Unsplash

It's the first Tuesday class. Amara and Dilnoza meet at the door. The form didn't say which room, so they look for the notice Samuel told them about.

👩🏻
Dilnoza
Here it is. "Classes meet every Tuesday and Thursday evening in the large room." Which one is the large room?
👩🏾
Amara
Not the first door. That's the supply closet. I already tried it.
👩🏻
Dilnoza
It also says, "Bring a pencil and a small notebook."
👩🏾
Amara
Small? Mine is huge. It's my son's old school notebook.
👩🏻
Dilnoza
I don't think they'll check. More pages, more English.
👩🏾
Amara
OK. Let's find that room before all the good seats are gone.

Now read the whole notice. Every word has a job. Some words name things, some show action, some describe, and some tell you when.

The notice on the bulletin board:

Free English classes start in September. Classes meet every Tuesday and Thursday evening in the large room. Bring a pencil and a small notebook.

nouns English, classes, September, room, pencil, notebook
verbs start, meet, bring
adjectives free, large, small
adverb every Tuesday and Thursday evening (a group of words that tells us when)

Quick guide:

Noun: person, place, thing, or idea. Can follow "a / an / the."

Verb: action or state. Changes for tense (start / started / starting).

Adjective: describes a noun. Ask: what kind? how many?

Adverb: describes a verb. Ask: how? when? how often?

Name the part of speech

Read the sentence. Choose the correct part of speech for the word in bold.

  1. "Dilnoza reads the <strong>notice</strong> on the board."

    Noun / Verb / Adjective / Adverb

    Answer / teacher checknoun
  2. "The classes <strong>meet</strong> every Tuesday."

    Noun / Verb / Adjective / Adverb

    Answer / teacher checkverb
  3. "They need a <strong>small</strong> notebook."

    Noun / Verb / Adjective / Adverb

    Answer / teacher checkadjective
  4. "Amara reads the notice <strong>carefully</strong>."

    Noun / Verb / Adjective / Adverb

    Answer / teacher checkadverb
  5. "The evening classes are <strong>free</strong>."

    Noun / Verb / Adjective / Adverb

    Answer / teacher checkadjective

Fix the sentence

Choose the correct word for each sentence. Sometimes the word in bold is already correct.

  1. "Dilnoza reads the notice <strong>careful</strong>."

    careful: an adjective, it describes a noun / carefully: an adverb, it describes a verb

    Answer / teacher checkcarefully
  2. "The room is <strong>largely</strong> and comfortable."

    large: an adjective, it describes a noun / largely: an adverb, it describes a verb

    Answer / teacher checklarge
  3. "Amara is a <strong>careful</strong> reader."

    careful: an adjective, it describes a noun / carefully: an adverb, it describes a verb

    Answer / teacher checkcareful

Build the sentence

Unscramble the words.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkAmara and Dilnoza read the notice together
  2. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkAmara's class meets on Tuesday and Thursday evenings

Write the word type

Read the notice again. Write the word type: noun, verb, adjective, or adverb.

  1. In "Free English classes start in September," what type of word is "start"?
    Answer / teacher checkverb
  2. In "Bring a small notebook," what type of word is "small"?
    Answer / teacher checkadjective

Guide mini-quiz

  1. Amara picks up a pencil at the registration desk. Which word is a noun?

    picks / pencil / at

    Answerpencil

    Pencil names a thing. Nouns name people, places, things, and ideas.

  2. Amara is talking about the class schedule. Which sentence is correct?

    "I am understanding the schedule." / "I understand the schedule." / "I understanding the schedule."

    Answer"I understand the schedule."

    Understand is a state verb, so it does not take the -ing form. Other state verbs: know, want, need, remember, like, have.

  3. "Samuel is a helpful neighbor in Amara's building." Which word is the adjective?

    Samuel / helpful / building

    Answerhelpful

    Helpful describes the noun neighbor. It answers 'what kind of neighbor?'

  4. Amara tells a friend about Dilnoza. Put the words in order.
    AnswerHer sister has a part-time job

    Adjectives go before the noun in English: a full-time job, not a job full-time.

  5. Three people describe themselves at the community center. Which sentence has an error?

    "I have two young children." / "I work hardly every day." / "I live in a small apartment."

    Answer"I work hardly every day."

    Hard is the correct adverb here, not hardly. 'I work hard' means with a lot of effort. 'Hardly' means almost not at all, the opposite meaning.

W3: Parts of Speech Guide

Weekly plan ·

Required lesson and practice

Nouns: naming the world around you

Scene  East Boston Community Center. Tuesday, 5:30 PM. Amara writes down her information. Photo: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash

Amara cleans patient rooms at a hospital. She works days and has two kids, so she can only study at night. Today she comes straight from work to sign up for a free English class. James works at the front desk.

🙋🏼
James
Hi. This is the registration desk. Can I get your name and address?
👩🏾
Amara
Amara Yusuf. My address is 24 Meridian Street, near the hospital.
🙋🏼
James
Thanks. Please fill out this form. You will also need a pencil and a notebook for class.
👩🏾
Amara
I have a notebook in my bag. Could I borrow a pencil?

Look at the words in bold: desk, name, address, street, hospital, form, pencil, notebook, bag. Each one is a name for a place or a thing. These words are nouns.

Nouns name people, places, things, and ideas. If you can say "a ___" or "the ___" in front of it, it is probably a noun.

person a volunteer, the teacher, Amara, a student
place the community center, Meridian Street, the second floor
thing a pencil, a notebook, the form, a bag
idea English, education, registration, progress

Thing or idea?

A thing is something you can touch: a pencil, a notebook, the form, a bag.

An idea is something you cannot touch. You can only think about it or feel it: English, education, registration, progress.

Ask yourself: can I pick it up with my hands? If no, it is an idea.

Singular and plural:

one class / two classes

a student / many students

Most nouns add -s or -es to become plural.

Spot the noun

Choose the noun in each sentence.

  1. Amara fills out a form at the community center.

    fills / form / out

    Answer / teacher checkform
  2. The volunteer explains each question carefully.

    explains / carefully / volunteer

    Answer / teacher checkvolunteer
  3. She carries a pencil and a notebook in her bag.

    carries / pencil / in

    Answer / teacher checkpencil

Person, place, thing, or idea?

What kind of noun is it? Remember: a thing is something you can touch. An idea is something you cannot touch.

  1. What kind of noun is the word 'hospital'?

    Person (who) / Place (where) / Thing (you can touch it) / Idea (you cannot touch it)

    Answer / teacher checkplace
  2. What kind of noun is the word 'education'?

    Person (who) / Place (where) / Thing (you can touch it) / Idea (you cannot touch it)

    Answer / teacher checkidea
  3. What kind of noun is the word 'notebook'?

    Person (who) / Place (where) / Thing (you can touch it) / Idea (you cannot touch it)

    Answer / teacher checkthing

Build the sentence

Put the words in the correct order.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkThe volunteer hands Amara a form
  2. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkThe supply closet is behind the first door

Singular or plural?

Write the plural form of the noun.

  1. one notebook / two ___
    Answer / teacher checknotebooks
  2. one box / three ___
    Answer / teacher checkboxes

Verbs: action verbs and state verbs

Samuel fixes things in Amara's building, and he volunteers at the center on Tuesdays. He helps Amara with her registration form. Look at what each of them does, and what is true about each of them.

Sort
Action verbs and state verbs
Action State
Samuel helps, fixes knows, understands
Amara fills out, writes wants, needs, has, knows

The words in bold in the table are verbs. But they are not all the same kind. Some are things you do. Some are things that are true about you.

There are two types of verbs. Action verbs describe things you do. State verbs describe things that are true about you, such as what you feel, know, have, or think.

Action verbs: things you do

action Samuel helps students every Tuesday. He explains the schedule.
action Amara fills out the form. She writes her address in the first box.

State verbs: things that are true

state Amara knows Samuel from her building. She remembers his face.
state She wants the evening class. She understands why it is a good fit.
state Amara has two children. She needs a class in the evening.

Why does this matter?

State verbs are almost never used in the continuous (-ing) form.

✗ I am knowing the answer.

✓ I know the answer.

Common state verbs: know, want, need, understand, remember, believe, like, love, hate, have, seem.

Can you do it right now?: Ask yourself: can I watch someone do this? If yes, it is probably an action verb (run, write, help). If no, it is probably a state verb (know, want, understand). You cannot watch someone 'know' something.

Action or state?

Choose the correct label for the verb in bold.

  1. Samuel <strong>helps</strong> new students every Tuesday.

    Action verb: you can watch someone do it / State verb: a feeling, a fact, or something in the mind

    Answer / teacher checkaction
  2. Amara <strong>knows</strong> Samuel from her building.

    Action verb: you can watch someone do it / State verb: a feeling, a fact, or something in the mind

    Answer / teacher checkstate
  3. She <strong>fills out</strong> the form at the registration desk.

    Action verb: you can watch someone do it / State verb: a feeling, a fact, or something in the mind

    Answer / teacher checkaction
  4. Amara <strong>wants</strong> an evening class.

    Action verb: you can watch someone do it / State verb: a feeling, a fact, or something in the mind

    Answer / teacher checkstate

Correct or not?

State verbs do not use the -ing form. Is each sentence correct?

  1. "I am knowing all the students in my class."

    Correct: this verb can use the -ing form. / Not correct: this verb cannot use the -ing form.

    Answer / teacher checkincorrect
  2. "Samuel is helping a student right now."

    Correct: this verb can use the -ing form. / Not correct: this verb cannot use the -ing form.

    Answer / teacher checkcorrect
  3. "She is wanting the evening class."

    Correct: this verb can use the -ing form. / Not correct: this verb cannot use the -ing form.

    Answer / teacher checkincorrect

Look at the table about Samuel and Amara.

    needs / has / fills out

    Answer / teacher checkfills out
  2. Look at the table. How many state verbs does Amara have in her row? Write a number.
    Answer / teacher check4,four

Fill in the verb

Write the correct form of the verb in parentheses.

    Answer / teacher checkwants

Adjectives: describing words

Dilnoza sits down next to Amara. She is a cashier at a supermarket, and she is signing up for the same class. The last part of the form is called "About You." Names of things are not enough here. They need to describe their lives. First, Dilnoza reads about a real person who moved to a new country. Look at the words that describe.

Famous person
Hamdi Ulukaya: A New Country

Hamdi Ulukaya grew up on a mountain in eastern Turkey, near the Euphrates River. Later, he moved to the United States, a new country. In 2005, he started Chobani, a yogurt company.

In 2016, he started Tent. Tent helps large businesses hire refugees. Today, it works with more than 500 of the world's largest employers. Ulukaya says, "The minute a refugee gets a job is the minute they stop being a refugee."

Photo: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, public domain. Sources: Tent: Hamdi Ulukaya, Tent: About

Adjectives describe nouns. They answer what kind? or how many? Adjectives usually come right before the noun they describe.

what kind Amara has a full-time job. She works in a busy hospital.
what kind They live in a new building on a quiet street.
how many Amara has two children. Dilnoza has three brothers.
how many The form has five sections. The first section asks for your name.

Adjective position:

a small apartment (adjective before noun)

The apartment is small. (adjective after is/are/was)

Find the adjective

Choose the adjective in each sentence.

  1. Amara has a full-time job at a busy hospital.

    job / busy / has

    Answer / teacher checkbusy
  2. Dilnoza lives in a small apartment with her sister.

    lives / apartment / small

    Answer / teacher checksmall
  3. Dilnoza has three brothers.

    has / three / brothers

    Answer / teacher checkthree

Read about Hamdi Ulukaya

Look at the reading.

  1. Look at the reading. Where did Hamdi Ulukaya grow up?

    In the United States / In eastern Turkey / In a city on the coast

    Answer / teacher checkeastern
  2. Look at the reading. In what year did he start Tent? Write the year.
    Answer / teacher check2016
  3. Look at the reading. Which word describes the noun "country"?

    started / later / new

    Answer / teacher checknew

Correct or not?

Is the adjective in the right place?

  1. "She has a schedule busy."

    Correct: the adjective is in the right place. / Not correct: the adjective is in the wrong place.

    Answer / teacher checkincorrect
  2. "The new building has two small rooms."

    Correct: the adjective is in the right place. / Not correct: the adjective is in the wrong place.

    Answer / teacher checkcorrect
  3. "They have children three."

    Correct: the adjective is in the right place. / Not correct: the adjective is in the wrong place.

    Answer / teacher checkincorrect

Build the sentence

Unscramble the words to make a correct sentence.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkDilnoza has a busy schedule this week
  2. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkThe form has five short sections

Write the adjective

Write the word that describes the noun.

  1. "Dilnoza has a busy schedule." Which word describes "schedule"?
    Answer / teacher checkbusy
  2. "The new building has two small rooms." Which word describes "rooms"?
    Answer / teacher checksmall

Adverbs: how, when, how often

On Saturday, it's cleanup day at Amara's building. Samuel is outside in work gloves, writing repairs on a clipboard. Amara tells him her kitchen sink is leaking again. Then she asks how his week works. This is what he tells her.

Chart
Samuel's week: how often?
always
100% Samuel always helps at the center on Tuesdays.
usually
80% He usually fixes a leak in one visit.
sometimes
40% He sometimes eats lunch at his desk.
rarely
10% He rarely takes a day off.
never
0% He never leaves a job unfinished.

"I can fix the sink on Monday," he says, and writes it down. Words like always tell us how often. Other words tell us when and how. They are all adverbs.

Adverbs describe verbs. They answer how?, when?, or how often? Many adverbs end in -ly (quickly, carefully, quietly). But not all of them do (well, hard, early, fast). A group of words can do the same job: every Tuesday, last year, after work.

how Samuel works quickly. He speaks English well.
when He finishes early. He comes after his shift on Tuesdays.
how often He volunteers every week. He always arrives on time.

Adjective or adverb? The question is: what does it describe?

Adjective Samuel is a quick worker. (describes the noun "worker")
Adverb Samuel works quickly. (describes the verb "works")
Adjective His English is good. (describes the noun "English")
Adverb He speaks English well. (describes the verb "speaks")

Careful: hard and hardly

Samuel works hard. (with a lot of effort)

Samuel hardly works. (almost never, the opposite meaning)

Adding -ly does not always make the adverb. Hardly is a different word with a different meaning.

good vs. well: Good is an adjective: his English is good. Well is an adverb: he speaks English well. This pair catches many learners, including native speakers.

Adjective or adverb?

Choose the correct word for each sentence.

  1. Samuel is a ___ worker. He fixes most things the same day. (quick / quickly)

    quick (adjective) / quickly (adverb)

    Answer / teacher checkquick
  2. He finishes his work very ___. He is always done before noon. (quick / quickly)

    quick (adjective) / quickly (adverb)

    Answer / teacher checkquickly
  3. Dilnoza speaks English ___. She practices every day. (good / well)

    good (adjective) / well (adverb)

    Answer / teacher checkwell
  4. Her pronunciation is ___. People understand her easily. (good / well)

    good (adjective) / well (adverb)

    Answer / teacher checkgood

Read the chart

Look at Samuel's chart.

  1. Look at Samuel's chart. Which sentence is true?

    Samuel never takes a day off. / Samuel rarely takes a day off. / Samuel always takes a day off.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  2. Look at Samuel's chart. He ___ eats lunch at his desk. (Write one word.)
    Answer / teacher checksometimes

Fill in the adverb

Write the adverb form of the word in parentheses.

  1. Samuel explains the form ___. Everyone understands. (clear)
    Answer / teacher checkclearly
  2. Amara listens ___ during the orientation. (careful)
    Answer / teacher checkcarefully

All four working together

Scene  Tuesday, 6:20 PM. The board by the door at the community center, full of flyers and notices. Photo: Zoshua Colah / Unsplash

It's the first Tuesday class. Amara and Dilnoza meet at the door. The form didn't say which room, so they look for the notice Samuel told them about.

👩🏻
Dilnoza
Here it is. "Classes meet every Tuesday and Thursday evening in the large room." Which one is the large room?
👩🏾
Amara
Not the first door. That's the supply closet. I already tried it.
👩🏻
Dilnoza
It also says, "Bring a pencil and a small notebook."
👩🏾
Amara
Small? Mine is huge. It's my son's old school notebook.
👩🏻
Dilnoza
I don't think they'll check. More pages, more English.
👩🏾
Amara
OK. Let's find that room before all the good seats are gone.

Now read the whole notice. Every word has a job. Some words name things, some show action, some describe, and some tell you when.

The notice on the bulletin board:

Free English classes start in September. Classes meet every Tuesday and Thursday evening in the large room. Bring a pencil and a small notebook.

nouns English, classes, September, room, pencil, notebook
verbs start, meet, bring
adjectives free, large, small
adverb every Tuesday and Thursday evening (a group of words that tells us when)

Quick guide:

Noun: person, place, thing, or idea. Can follow "a / an / the."

Verb: action or state. Changes for tense (start / started / starting).

Adjective: describes a noun. Ask: what kind? how many?

Adverb: describes a verb. Ask: how? when? how often?

Name the part of speech

Read the sentence. Choose the correct part of speech for the word in bold.

  1. "Dilnoza reads the <strong>notice</strong> on the board."

    Noun / Verb / Adjective / Adverb

    Answer / teacher checknoun
  2. "The classes <strong>meet</strong> every Tuesday."

    Noun / Verb / Adjective / Adverb

    Answer / teacher checkverb
  3. "They need a <strong>small</strong> notebook."

    Noun / Verb / Adjective / Adverb

    Answer / teacher checkadjective
  4. "Amara reads the notice <strong>carefully</strong>."

    Noun / Verb / Adjective / Adverb

    Answer / teacher checkadverb
  5. "The evening classes are <strong>free</strong>."

    Noun / Verb / Adjective / Adverb

    Answer / teacher checkadjective

Fix the sentence

Choose the correct word for each sentence. Sometimes the word in bold is already correct.

  1. "Dilnoza reads the notice <strong>careful</strong>."

    careful: an adjective, it describes a noun / carefully: an adverb, it describes a verb

    Answer / teacher checkcarefully
  2. "The room is <strong>largely</strong> and comfortable."

    large: an adjective, it describes a noun / largely: an adverb, it describes a verb

    Answer / teacher checklarge
  3. "Amara is a <strong>careful</strong> reader."

    careful: an adjective, it describes a noun / carefully: an adverb, it describes a verb

    Answer / teacher checkcareful

Build the sentence

Unscramble the words.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkAmara and Dilnoza read the notice together
  2. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkAmara's class meets on Tuesday and Thursday evenings

Write the word type

Read the notice again. Write the word type: noun, verb, adjective, or adverb.

  1. In "Free English classes start in September," what type of word is "start"?
    Answer / teacher checkverb
  2. In "Bring a small notebook," what type of word is "small"?
    Answer / teacher checkadjective

Guide mini-quiz

  1. Amara picks up a pencil at the registration desk. Which word is a noun?

    picks / pencil / at

    Answerpencil

    Pencil names a thing. Nouns name people, places, things, and ideas.

  2. Amara is talking about the class schedule. Which sentence is correct?

    "I am understanding the schedule." / "I understand the schedule." / "I understanding the schedule."

    Answer"I understand the schedule."

    Understand is a state verb, so it does not take the -ing form. Other state verbs: know, want, need, remember, like, have.

  3. "Samuel is a helpful neighbor in Amara's building." Which word is the adjective?

    Samuel / helpful / building

    Answerhelpful

    Helpful describes the noun neighbor. It answers 'what kind of neighbor?'

  4. Amara tells a friend about Dilnoza. Put the words in order.
    AnswerHer sister has a part-time job

    Adjectives go before the noun in English: a full-time job, not a job full-time.

  5. Three people describe themselves at the community center. Which sentence has an error?

    "I have two young children." / "I work hardly every day." / "I live in a small apartment."

    Answer"I work hardly every day."

    Hard is the correct adverb here, not hardly. 'I work hard' means with a lot of effort. 'Hardly' means almost not at all, the opposite meaning.

W4: Verb Forms + Your Study Toolkit

Weekly plan ·

Required lesson and practice

The wrong lunch bag · five verb forms

Scene  Tuesday, class break. Carlos opens his lunch bag and finds a surprise. Photo: Ilya Sonin / Unsplash

Catch up with Carlos and Fernanda. Read for the message first.

👩🏾
Fernanda
Break time. What did you bring for dinner tonight?
👨🏽
Carlos
A sandwich. Wait, this isn’t my bag. There’s no food, just a little box.
👩🏾
Fernanda
Is that a ring box? Whose bag is that?
👨🏽
Carlos
I think it’s Mark’s bag. He works with me at the restaurant. We use the same staff fridge.
👩🏾
Fernanda
Call him. Maybe he is looking for it.
👨🏽
Carlos
I don’t have his number. But my sister Sarah is working there right now. I’ll text her.

Carlos preps food at La Palma in the mornings. Mark is a line cook there, and Sarah is a server. Notice works and working, then compare all five forms below.

Five labels, one verb. The labels help you find and check a form.

  • V1: work · the base form
  • V1-s: works · with he/she/it in the present
  • V-ing: working · as in “She’s working now.”
  • V2: worked · a past form
  • V3: worked · as in “I’ve worked that shift.”

Try it: Say the five forms. Look away and try again. Check just the one you forget.

Know the codes

Read for the message. Choose an answer or type the missing word.

  1. Why is Carlos surprised at the break?

    He is late for his restaurant shift. / His bag has a ring box, not his dinner. / His sister forgot her lunch at home.

    Answer / teacher checkdinner
  2. Where is Sarah right now?

    At the restaurant. She is working. / At home. She has finished work. / At class with Carlos.

    Answer / teacher checkno
  3. Carlos tells Fernanda: “Mark ___ with me at the restaurant.” (work)
    Answer / teacher checkworks

Mark is looking everywhere · V1, V1-s, V-ing

Scene  Still on break, Carlos texts his sister Sarah at the restaurant. Photo: Patrick Tomasso / Unsplash
👨🏽
Carlos
Emergency! I took the wrong lunch bag from the fridge. There’s a ring inside. Is it Mark’s?
👩🏻
Sarah
Yes. Mark brings that blue bag every day. And tonight he wants to ask Lisa to marry him.
👨🏽
Carlos
Oh no. Class finishes at eight. Where is he now?
👩🏻
Sarah
He’s looking everywhere in the kitchen. I’m serving tables, so I can’t leave. Meet Mark at the café at eight.

Sarah talks about Mark’s usual routine and what is happening right now. Have you ever taken the wrong bag, coat, or phone?

Quick form check: I/you/we/they bring; he/she/it brings. For an action in progress, use am/is/are + V-ing: “He’s looking everywhere.”

Your reply: “I usually ___ before class. Right now, I’m ___.” Use your own details, then say it again without looking.

Spot the form

Continue the text conversation. For a blank, type only the missing word.

  1. Sarah is busy at this moment. Which text tells Carlos what is happening now?

    I serve tables every evening. / I served tables last night. / I’m serving tables. I’ll text you later.

    Answer / teacher checknow
  2. Sarah texts: “Mark never ___ his lunch bag. He’s checking every shelf!” (forget)
    Answer / teacher checkforgets
  3. Carlos replies: “Tell him not to worry. I am ___ an alarm for eight o’clock.” (set)
    Answer / teacher checksetting

Just in time · V2 and V3

Scene  8:05 at the café. Mark runs in, out of breath. Photo: Nathan Dumlao / Unsplash
👨🏿
Mark
Carlos! I’ve looked everywhere for that bag!
👨🏽
Carlos
Sorry. I grabbed the wrong one this morning. I opened it at break. Here’s your ring.
👨🏿
Mark
Thank you. Now I have to tell you something. I ate your sandwich at lunch.
👨🏽
Carlos
So I’ve missed dinner, but I saved your big night. Go, Mark! You have twenty minutes.

Carlos tells what happened this morning. Mark and Carlos also connect the past to right now. The examples below show how V2 and V3 work with the same verb.

Quick form check: “I grabbed the bag this morning” uses V2. “I’ve looked everywhere” uses have + V3. I’ve means I have.

For regular verbs, V2 and V3 both end in -ed. They look the same; the words around them help you understand the meaning.

Try it: Tell a partner one thing you did yesterday. Check the verb and tell it again. You can invent details.

Choose V2 or V3

Think about what each person means. Type only the missing word.

  1. Carlos says sorry to Mark: “I’ve worked at La Palma for four years. This is my first mix-up!” What does he mean?

    He stopped working there four years ago. / He started four years ago and still works there. / He will start there in four years.

    Answer / teacher checkstill
  2. Carlos tells Mark: “I ___ class with your ring in my bag!” (start)
    Answer / teacher checkstarted
  3. Mark laughs: “I have ___ that blue bag for three years. I need a new one!” (use)
    Answer / teacher checkused

She said yes! · Be and have

Scene  Later that night, Carlos sits down to do his online homework. Then a group chat from Sarah pops up. Photo: Christina @ wocintechchat.com / Unsplash
👩🏻
Sarah
Big news. Mark is engaged. Lisa said yes at 8:30!
👨🏽
Carlos
I am so happy for them. I’m also very hungry.
👨🏿
Mark
Lisa has the ring, and I have a sandwich for you. Thank you, Carlos!
👩🏻
Sarah
You were a hero tonight, Carlos. Take the right bag tomorrow.
👨🏽
Carlos
I’ve been hungry since six. I’ve had enough surprises for one week!

Be and have change in special ways. Don’t add -ed.

Form be have
V1 be have
V1-s is has
V-ing being having
V2 was / were had
V3 been had

In present statements, use I am, he/she/it is, you/we/they are.

Join the chat: “Today I am ___. Yesterday I was ___. I have ___.” Say or write your own reply. You can invent details.

Check one thing: “Lisa have the ring.” → “Lisa has the ring.” With she, use has. Now check one verb in your reply and try again. Return to two forms tomorrow.

be and have on the quiz

Help everyone finish their messages. Type only the missing word.

  1. Sarah types, “Lisa have the ring now.” Help her fix the message.

    Lisa has the ring now. / Lisa having the ring now. / Lisa have the ring now.

    Answer / teacher checkhas
  2. Mark replies: “Lisa and I ___ both so nervous at dinner!” (be)
    Answer / teacher checkwere
  3. Carlos texts: “I’ve ___ a crazy day. Five minutes of practice is enough tonight.” (have)
    Answer / teacher checkhad

Guide mini-quiz

  1. Sarah explains the mix-up: “Mark ___ his lunch in the staff fridge every morning.” (leave)

    leave / leaves / leaving

    Answerleaves

    This is his usual routine. With Mark (he), use leaves.

  2. Sarah texts Carlos from work: “I am ___ tables now. Mark will meet you at the café!” (serve)
    Answerserving

    Use am + V-ing for an action in progress: I am serving tables. Drop the final e in serve before adding -ing.

  3. Carlos is home now. Which message needs a correction?

    I was nervous in class today. / I am home with a good story now. / I be ready to practice now.

    AnswerI be ready to practice now.

    Be is the base form. With I in a present statement, use am: I am ready to practice now.

  4. The next day, a new coworker at La Palma asks Carlos, “When did you start here?” Put his answer in order.
    AnswerI have worked here for four years

    After have/has, use V3. This connects past experience to the present.

  5. Sarah writes to the group chat about Lisa right now. Which message is correct?

    She has the ring now. / She have the ring now. / She had the ring yesterday.

    AnswerShe has the ring now.

    She has tells us about now. She had tells us about the past. With she, use has instead of have.

Week 4 Quiz · required
  1. be → V1-s (he/she/it)
    Answeris

    V1-s (he/she/it) of be: is.

  2. be → V-ing
    Answerbeing

    V-ing of be: being.

  3. be → V2 (past) (give both forms, separated by /)
    Answerwas/were / were/was

    V2 (past) of be: was/were.

  4. be → V3 (past participle)
    Answerbeen

    V3 (past participle) of be: been.

  5. have → V1-s (he/she/it)
    Answerhas

    V1-s (he/she/it) of have: has.

  6. have → V-ing
    Answerhaving

    V-ing of have: having.

  7. have → V2 (past)
    Answerhad

    V2 (past) of have: had.

  8. have → V3 (past participle)
    Answerhad

    V3 (past participle) of have: had.

  9. She ___ going to the Salvadoran festival this Saturday. (be)
    Answeris

    She is going to the Salvadoran festival this Saturday. (be)

  10. He ___ a Honda Civic before he crashed it. (have)
    Answerhad

    He had a Honda Civic before he crashed it. (have)

  11. Which word means “to give your attention to one thing”?

    correct / remember / focus

    Answerfocus

    focus: to give your attention to one thing. Focus on one sentence at a time.

  12. You learned a rule. Now _____ it by using it in a new sentence.

    apply / remember / notice / focus

    Answerapply

    apply: to use what you learned. Apply the rule by writing a new sentence about yourself.

  13. In “The helpful teacher has a book,” which word describes the teacher?

    teacher / helpful / has

    Answerhelpful

    Helpful is an adjective. It describes the noun teacher.

  14. Fix one word: “She have a brother in Colombia.” Write the complete sentence.
    AnswerShe has a brother in Colombia.

    With she, have becomes has.

W5: Questions That Get Real Answers

Weekly plan ·

Required lesson and practice

Questions for smarter digital habits

Scene  East Boston. Rosa asks her neighbor Sarah about an unexpected email. Photo: Priscilla Du Preez / Unsplash

This week, use questions to talk about digital habits: checking messages, finding files, protecting your information, and asking for help. Rosa has an email that does not seem right.

Notice how Rosa and Sarah use questions to understand the message and decide what to do.

👩🏾
Rosa
What do you do when you get a strange email?
🧑🏽
Sarah
I don't click anything. Who is it from?
👩🏾
Rosa
It says it's from my bank. It wants me to click a link to keep my account open.
🧑🏽
Sarah
That sounds suspicious. Where do you usually check your account?
👩🏾
Rosa
In the bank's app. I'll open that instead. If I need help, I can call the number on my bank card.
WHO asks about a person
WHAT asks about a thing or idea
WHERE asks about a place
WHEN asks about a time
WHY asks about a reason
HOW asks about a way, a method, or a detail

Match the question word

Read each question. Which word asks that kind of information?

  1. "___ is the sender of this email?" (You want to know the person's name.)

    Who / What / Where

    Answer / teacher checkwho
  2. "___ does the video call start?" (You want to know the time.)

    Why / When / How

    Answer / teacher checkwhen
  3. "___ is the Downloads folder?" (You want to know the place.)

    What / Who / Where

    Answer / teacher checkwhere
  4. "___ did you delete that message?" (You want to know the reason.)

    Why / When / How

    Answer / teacher checkwhy
  5. ___ do you join a video call? (Ask about the method: with an app or a website.)
    Answer / teacher checkHow,how

Who, What, Where: the basics

Scene  At a computer. Sarah helps her neighbor Amara find a downloaded job application. Photo: Jonathan Borba / Unsplash
👩🏿
Amara
I can't find the form I downloaded. Where is it?
🧑🏽
Sarah
Let's look in your Downloads folder. What is the file called?
👩🏿
Amara
Job application. There it is! Who is the contact person?
🧑🏽
Sarah
James in the hiring office. His email address is on the job posting.

For the questions below, choose the pattern that matches the verb.

  • With be: Who is the sender? Where are my downloads?
  • With most action verbs in the present simple: What do you share online? Where does she save her files?

The pattern:

With BE

Wh- word + am / is / are + subject

Where is the file?   Who is the sender?

With DO / DOES / DID

Wh- word + do / does / did + subject + base verb

What do you do?   Where does she work?

For the past, use did with the base verb: When did you download it? Not did you downloaded.

Common mistake to avoid:

✗ Where you save your files?   (missing do/does)

✓ Where do you save your files?

Fix the question

One word is missing or wrong. Choose the correct question.

  1. "Where you shop online?" How do you fix this question?

    Where you are shopping online? / Where do you shop online? / Where shops you online?

    Answer / teacher checkb
  2. "What is the file's name?" Is this question correct?

    Yes, correct as written. / No. Should be: What does the file's name?

    Answer / teacher checkcorrect
  3. "What do your sister share online?" How do you fix this question?

    What does your sister share online? / What is your sister share online? / What your sister shares online?

    Answer / teacher checka
  4. "Where ___ you save your files?" (Fill in the missing helper verb.)
    Answer / teacher checkdo

Build the question

Put the words in the right order.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkWhere does Amara save her files
  2. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkWhat is the file name

When and How: time and details

Scene  A community center in East Boston. Nadine asks a tech helper how to save her photos. Photo: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash
👩‍💼
Tech helper
When did you last save a copy of your photos on another device?
👩🏿
Nadine
I haven't done that. How do I copy them to my laptop?
👩‍💼
Tech helper
You can connect your phone with a USB cable. Do you have yours?
👩🏿
Nadine
Yes. How long does it take?
👩‍💼
Tech helper
It depends on the number of photos. Let's try a few.

When asks about a time. How asks about a method or a detail.

How is powerful because it combines with other words to ask specific questions.

When a point in time

When did the message arrive? When does the download finish?

How a method or way

How do you join the video call? (through the app)

How long a duration

How long does the download take? (two minutes)

How often a frequency

How often do you check your email? (twice a day)

How far a distance

How far is the computer from the Wi-Fi router? (ten feet)

How + another word = a specific question: How long, how often, how far, how much, how many. Each one narrows the question. You will keep adding to this list all year.

When or How?

Read what the person wants to know. Choose the correct question word or phrase.

  1. You want to know if the online meeting is Monday or Tuesday. You ask: "___ does the online meeting start?"

    When / How / How long

    Answer / teacher checkwhen
  2. You want to know if the video is 6 minutes or 12 minutes. You ask: "___ is the video?"

    When / How long / How often

    Answer / teacher checkhow long
  3. You want to know if your classmate checks email every day or once a week. You ask: "___ do you check your email?"

    How far / How often / When

    Answer / teacher checkhow often

Fill in the question word

Write the correct question word. Use: When, How, How long, How often, How far.

  1. "___ did you create this account?" (You want to know the month or year.)
    Answer / teacher checkWhen,when
  2. "___ do you join the video call?" (You want to know the method: through an app or a website.)
    Answer / teacher checkHow,how

Why: giving and asking for reasons

Scene  During a class break. Linh checks what an app can access on her phone. Photo: Kübra Arslaner / Unsplash
👩🏾
Linh
Why does this flashlight app want my location?
🧑🏽
Classmate
That's strange. What happens if you say no?
👩🏾
Linh
It still works. I'm turning off location access.
🧑🏽
Classmate
Why don't you use the flashlight that came with your phone?
👩🏾
Linh
Because I didn't know I had one! Can you show me?

Why asks for a reason. You can begin your answer with because.

Why + do/does/did + subject + base verb? Why did she close the app?
With be: Why + am/is/are + subject + detail? Why is the app slow?

question Why do you keep your passwords private?
answer Because I want to protect my accounts.
question Why did she close the website?
answer Because it asked for information she did not want to share.

Short answer (informal):

You do not have to repeat the full question in your answer.

Why do you silence your phone at night?   Because I need to sleep.

Complete the answer

Choose the best answer to each Why question.

  1. "Why do you turn off notifications at night?" Which answer fits?

    Because I need to sleep without interruptions. / I turn them off at ten. / The setting is under Notifications.

    Answer / teacher checka
  2. "Why did Linh turn off location access for the flashlight app?" Which answer fits?

    She downloaded the app on Tuesday. / Because the flashlight works without knowing her location. / The flashlight button is on the screen.

    Answer / teacher checkb

Build the Why question

Unscramble the words to make a correct Why question.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkWhy do you use different passwords
  2. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkWhy did he delete the email
  3. "Why do you check the sender before replying?" A good answer usually starts with ___.
    Answer / teacher checkbecause,Because

Checking a suspicious message

Scene  After work in East Boston. Diego shows Fernanda an unexpected delivery text. Photo: Nathana Rebouças / Unsplash

Diego has not ordered anything, but a text says he owes a delivery fee. He and Fernanda talk through what to do before he clicks anything.

🧑🏽
Diego
I got a text about a package. It says I need to pay a delivery fee.
👩🏽
Fernanda
What did you order?
🧑🏽
Diego
Nothing. That's why I'm confused.
👩🏽
Fernanda
Then don't use the link. Where is the option to report the message?
🧑🏽
Diego
Here, under the menu. I'll report it as junk.
👩🏽
Fernanda
Good. How often do you get these texts? I've had three this week.

Choose the pattern that fits your question:
Be: Where is the file?
Do / does / did + base verb: What did you download?
Be + verb-ing: What are you downloading?
Sometimes who or what is the subject: Who sent this message? What happens? These questions do not need do, does, or did.

Two mistakes to watch for:

Missing helper verb

✗ Where you save your photos?

✓ Where do you save your photos?

Wrong word order (subject before helper)

✗ What you are downloading?

✓ What are you downloading?

One question leads to another: Your turn: Ask a classmate one question about their phone habits. Try: How often do you ___? Listen to their answer, then ask one follow-up question. You can practice aloud by yourself too.

Spot the mistake

Three people wrote questions. One of them made an error. Find it.

  1. Which question has a mistake?

    Where does Fernanda save her photos? / Why did Diego report the text? / What you do with strange emails?

    Answer / teacher checkc
  2. Which question has a mistake?

    When did she download the app? / Who is the sender? / How she checks her email?

    Answer / teacher checkc
  3. "___ did Diego report the text?" (You want to know the reason.)
    Answer / teacher checkWhy,why

Build the question

Unscramble the words to make a correct question.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkHow do you report a message
  2. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkWhy did Diego report the text
  3. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkWhen does the video call start

Guide mini-quiz

  1. Fill in the question word: ___ did she close the pop-up? Because it asked for her password.
    AnswerWhy

    Why asks for a reason. Because introduces a reason.

  2. Which question correctly asks about the person who created an app?

    Who created this app? / Who did created this app? / Who created app this?

    AnswerWho created this app?

    Who asks about a person. Here, who is the subject, so we do not add did.

  3. Your answer is: Twice a day. Which question were you asked?

    How long is the video? / How do you open the app? / How often do you check email?

    AnswerHow often do you check email?

    How often asks about frequency: how many times something happens.

  4. A classmate asks about an online meeting. Put the words in order to make the question.
    AnswerWhen does the online meeting start

    Question word order: Wh- word + do/does + subject + main verb.

  5. Linh wants to know if a tutorial video is 2 minutes long or 20 minutes long. She asks:

    How often is the video? / How long is the video? / How far is the video?

    AnswerHow long is the video?

    How long asks about duration. Two minutes and twenty minutes are lengths of time.

W6: Your Week in English

Weekly plan ·

Required lesson and practice

How often do you...?

Scene  Outside the community center, Tuesday evening. Rosa came to class 30 minutes late. Photo: Sam / Unsplash
🧕🏾
Fatima
Rosa! You're never late. What happened tonight?
👩🏽
Rosa
The 116. I always take it at 5:15, but tonight I waited 40 minutes.
🧕🏾
Fatima
It's detoured this week. The stop moved two blocks up, next to the pharmacy.
👩🏽
Rosa
How do you know that?
🧕🏾
Fatima
The MBTA app. I usually check it before I leave at 5:30. Don't you?
👩🏽
Rosa
I never use apps for the bus. I just walk to the stop and wait.

Adverbs of frequency tell us how often something happens. They go before the main verb, but after the verb be.

Chart
How often? From 100% to 0%
always
100% I always take the bus on Tuesdays.
usually
80% She usually checks the app before she leaves.
often
60% They often take the same bus to class.
sometimes
40% He sometimes misses the bus.
rarely
10% We rarely take a taxi.
never
0% I never click links in strange texts.

Position rule

Before a main verb: I always take the bus.

After the verb be: She is sometimes late.

Timeline labels: Present Simple (present)

Adverb position

  1. The 116 bus <strong>is always</strong> crowded at 5:30. Where does 'always' go in this sentence?

    Correct. After 'is' because 'be' comes first. / Wrong. It should go before 'is'. / Wrong. It should go at the end.

    Answer / teacher checkcorrect
  2. Fatima ___ checks the app and leaves home at 5:30. Which adverb means she does it about 80% of the time?

    always / usually / rarely

    Answer / teacher checkusually
  3. "She sometimes is late." Is this sentence correct?

    Yes, it is correct. / No. With 'be', the adverb comes after: 'She is sometimes late.'

    Answer / teacher checkincorrect

Build the sentence

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkFatima never misses her English class
  2. Fatima's husband drives a delivery truck. He ___ takes the bus. (Fill in the blank with an adverb meaning almost never.)
    Answer / teacher checkrarely

I work, I take the bus, I don't drive

Jessica at the community center's tech help desk helped Rosa fill out a sign-up form. The form asked: "What does your week look like?" This is her answer.

Schedule

Rosa doesn't have a car. She works at a hotel by the airport.

Present Simple describes routines, habits, and facts that are true week after week.

Positive

I / You / We / They + base verb: I work every day.
He / She / It + verb + -s / -es: She works every day.

Negative

I / You / We / They: I don't work on Sundays.
He / She / It: She doesn't work on Sundays.

Question

Do you work on Saturdays?
Does she work on Saturdays?

Watch out

With doesn't, the main verb goes back to the base form. She doesn't work (not works).

Timeline labels: Present Simple (present)

Choose the correct form

  1. Look at Rosa's week. Rosa ___ to class on Tuesday and Thursday evenings. (come)

    come / comes / is coming

    Answer / teacher checkcomes
  2. Look at Rosa's week. Which sentence is true?

    Rosa works on Saturdays. / Rosa doesn't work on Saturdays. / Rosa doesn't take the bus on Mondays.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  3. "She don't have time for homework." Is this sentence correct?

    Yes, it is correct. / No. She is third person singular, so it should be 'She doesn't have.'

    Answer / teacher checkincorrect
  4. ___ Rosa take the bus to work?

    Do / Does / Is

    Answer / teacher checkDoes

Build the sentence

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkRosa doesn't work on Sundays
  2. Look at Rosa's week. She ___ (not / go) to class on Mondays. Use 'doesn't' + base verb.
    Answer / teacher checkdoesn't go,does not go
  3. Look at Rosa's week. What does Rosa do on Sundays? She ___ her family. (call)
    Answer / teacher checkcalls

Every day, twice a week...

Famous person
Ellen Ochoa: A Routine in Space

In 1993, Ellen Ochoa became the first Hispanic woman in space. She flew on the space shuttle Discovery. She went to space four times, and on her first trip, she played her flute in space! Later, she became the director of NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston.

Today, astronauts live and work on the International Space Station. They have a routine, just like us. They exercise for at least two hours every day because life in space makes muscles and bones weak. The station goes around the Earth 16 times a day, so astronauts see a sunrise about every 90 minutes.

Photo: NASA, 1999, public domain. Sources: NASA: Ellen Ochoa, NASA: Space Station Facts

Time expressions say when or how often something happens. They usually go at the beginning or end of a sentence.

how often I take the bus every day.
how often She gets fake toll texts twice a week.
which day He works on Saturdays.
which day We have class on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
time of day In the morning, I check the bus app.
how often She reloads her CharlieCard once a month.

Notice

Adverbs of frequency go inside the sentence (before the verb). Time expressions like every day or on Mondays go at the start or end.

Choose the right phrase

  1. Look at the reading. Astronauts on the space station exercise for at least two hours ___.

    every day / once a week / twice a month

    Answer / teacher checkevery day
  2. Look at the reading. The space station goes around the Earth ___ times a day. How many?

    1 / 16 / 90

    Answer / teacher check16
  3. Rosa reloads her CharlieCard ___. Which phrase means one time per month?

    twice a week / once a month / on Tuesdays

    Answer / teacher checkonce a month
  4. "In the morning I check the bus app." Is the time expression in the right place?

    Yes. Time expressions can go at the start of the sentence. / No. Time expressions can only go at the end.

    Answer / teacher checkyes

Build the sentence

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkI take the bus to work every morning
  2. Rosa doesn't work ___ Saturdays. (Use one preposition.)
    Answer / teacher checkon

Walk one block. Don't wait here.

On Tuesday, Jessica helped Rosa download the bus app. On Wednesday morning, this alert is on her phone.

Bus app alert
Route 116: detour this week
1 Don't wait at the stop on Meridian Street. The 116 doesn't stop there this week.
2 Walk one block to the pharmacy.
3 Wait at the temporary stop next to the pharmacy.
4 Check the app for bus times.
5 Don't run after the bus. The next one comes in 15 minutes.
Valentina, Rosa's neighbor, doesn't have the app.

An imperative tells someone what to do. Start with the base verb. There is no subject: Walk one block. (not You walk one block.)

do Take the 116. Turn left at the corner.
don't Don't + base verb: Don't click the link. Don't pay.
polite Please + imperative: Please sit down.

Watch out

Say Don't + base verb. Not Not go, not Don't to go, not Don't going.

Read the alert

  1. Look at the bus alert. Where does Rosa get the 116 this week?

    At her usual stop on Meridian Street / One block away, by the pharmacy / At the hotel by the airport

    Answer / teacher checkb
  2. Look at the bus alert. Rosa misses a bus. How many minutes until the next one?

    5 / 15 / 60

    Answer / teacher check15
  3. Which sentence is a correct imperative?

    You turn right at the bank. / Turn right at the bank. / Turning right at the bank.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  4. "Not stand near the door." What is wrong?

    Nothing is wrong. / Not correct. Use don't + base verb: 'Don't stand near the door.'

    Answer / teacher checkincorrect
  5. A sign on the bus says: "Please ___ your seat to older people." (give)
    Answer / teacher checkgive

Build the sentence

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkPlease don't eat on the bus

My Weekly Routine

Scene  Outside Rosa's building on Meridian Street, Saturday evening. Her neighbor Valentina stops her. Photo: Clay Banks / Unsplash
👩🏾
Valentina
Rosa, wait. I got a text. It says I owe $6.95 for a toll. Should I pay it?
👩🏽
Rosa
Do you have a car?
👩🏾
Valentina
No. I always take the bus. And I missed class Thursday. The 116 never came.
👩🏽
Rosa
It's detoured. The stop is next to the pharmacy this week. I usually check the app now.
👩🏾
Valentina
You? The app? On Tuesday you didn't even have it.
👩🏽
Rosa
A lot can change in a week. And that text is fake. Don't pay it. Delete it.

Put it all together: adverbs of frequency + present simple + time expressions tell people about your week. Imperatives help a friend.

Rosa's week, in her own words:

I work five days a week at a hotel by the airport. I always take the 116 in the morning. I come to English class twice a week, on Tuesdays and Thursdays. This week the bus stop is next to the pharmacy. Now I usually check the app before I leave. I never click links in texts about tolls. I don't even have a car. My advice? Get the app, and don't pay fake tolls.

Great work this week: You now know how to talk about your weekly routine in English using adverbs of frequency, present simple, and time expressions. You can also give simple instructions with imperatives. Next week: making suggestions.

Putting it together

  1. Which sentence uses all the right grammar?

    She always is cook dinner every day. / She always cooks dinner every day. / She cooks always dinner every day.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  2. Valentina waited at the old bus stop on Thursday. What can Rosa tell her?

    Not wait at the Meridian Street stop. / Don't wait at the Meridian Street stop. / You don't waiting at the Meridian Street stop.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  3. Valentina got a text about a $6.95 toll. She doesn't have a car. What is the best advice?

    Pay it today. / Delete it. It's fake. / Click the link and check.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  4. Valentina doesn't have a car. She ___ the bus. (always / take)
    Answer / teacher checkalways takes

Build the sentences

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkI usually clean the house on Saturdays
  2. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkDon't wait for the bus in the street

Guide mini-quiz

  1. A coworker asks Rosa about her coffee habit at work. Which answer is correct?

    I drink always coffee at work. / I always drink coffee at work. / Always I drink coffee at work.

    AnswerI always drink coffee at work.

    Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb: I always drink.

  2. Fill in the blank: "Rosa ___ to class on Tuesdays and Thursdays." (come: he/she/it form)
    Answercomes

    With he/she/it in present simple, add -s: come → comes.

  3. "She don't work on Sundays." What is wrong with this sentence?

    Nothing is wrong. / Should be 'doesn't' because 'she' is third person singular. / Should be 'didn't' because it happened in the past.

    AnswerShould be 'doesn't' because 'she' is third person singular.

    With he/she/it in present simple negatives, use doesn't, not don't.

  4. Fatima gives a new classmate directions to the classroom. Put the words in order.
    AnswerTake the stairs and turn left

    Imperatives start with the base verb: Take..., turn...

  5. Rosa says about the 116 this week: "It is always late." Where does 'always' go in this sentence?

    It should go before 'is': It always is late. / It should go at the end: It is late always. / It is in the right place. With 'be', the adverb comes after.

    AnswerIt is in the right place. With 'be', the adverb comes after.

    After the verb 'be', adverbs of frequency follow it: It is always late.
