W7: Zero + First Conditional: If This, Then That

Weekly plan ·

Required lesson and practice

Zero Conditional: If It's Always True

Bring back: First, build will + base verb: I will call. She will help. After if, use the present simple: If I need help, I will call.

Scene  La Palma Restaurant, East Boston. Monday morning before the lunch rush. The manager, Scott, checks his clipboard. Photo: Stefan Vladimirov / Unsplash

Carlos is a prep cook at La Palma. He became a U.S. citizen in June, and this November is his first election. Election Day is Tuesday, November 3.

👨🏽
Carlos
Scott, can I come in at 11 on Election Day? It's my first time voting.
👨🏼‍💼
Scott
Congratulations. If you need a day off, you ask two weeks ahead. A morning is easier.
👨🏽
Carlos
Just the morning. The polls open at 7. I'll be here by 11.
👨🏼‍💼
Scott
Write it on the request sheet. My wife votes at 7 every year. If you go early, the line is short.
👨🏽
Carlos
And if the line is long and I'm late?
👨🏼‍💼
Scott
Same as any day. If you're running late, you call me before your shift starts.

Zero Conditional = a fact that is always true. A rule, a policy, a natural consequence. Both verbs are present simple.
If + present simple, present simple.

always true If you are in line by 8 PM, you get to vote.
always true If you go early, the line is short.
always true If water boils, it turns to steam.
always true If you move, you update your voter registration.

The comma rule: If + condition first, then result. You can also flip it: You get to vote if you are in line by 8 PM. (No comma when the result comes first.)

Timeline labels: If + present (present) → result (present) (present)

Is it a rule or a fact?

Choose the correct answer based on the meaning.

  1. Scott says this is always true at the restaurant. Which sentence fits the Zero Conditional?

    If you want a weekend off, you will tell Scott a month ahead. / If you want a weekend off, you tell Scott a month ahead. / If you want a weekend off, you told Scott a month ahead.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  2. Which sentence is the Zero Conditional?

    If Carlos goes at 7, he will be at work by 11. / If Carlos went at 7, he would be at work by 11. / If you bring your ID, check-in is faster.

    Answer / teacher checkc
  3. Fill in the blank with the correct form: If your name ___ (be) on the voter list, you get a ballot.
    Answer / teacher checkis

Build the sentence

Unscramble the words to make a correct Zero Conditional sentence.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkIf you work on Sunday you get a free meal

First Conditional: Real Future Plans

It's Thursday night. Carlos just got home from La Palma. His wife, Ana, went through the mail and made a to-do list for him. Look at the list.

Carlos's list
Before the election
✅ Ask Scott for Election Day morning off
⬜ Pay the electric bill ($190)
⬜ Register to vote online (deadline: October 24)
⬜ Pick up one extra shift

First Conditional = a real situation that might happen. The result is in the future.
If + present simple, will + base verb.

real future If Carlos picks up an extra shift, he will pay the electric bill.
real future If he doesn't register by October 24, he won't vote this year.
real future If the website asks for your license number, read it from your wallet.
real future If he registers tonight, he will be ready to vote early.

Important: In the if-part, never use will.
Correct: If he picks up the shift...
Wrong: If he will pick up the shift...

Timeline labels: If + present (present) → will + base verb (future)

Read the list

Look at Carlos's list above, then choose the best answer.

  1. Look at the list. Which thing has Carlos already done?

    He asked for the morning off. / He paid the electric bill. / He registered to vote.

    Answer / teacher checka
  2. Carlos has NOT registered yet. Which sentence about his plan is correct?

    If Carlos registers tonight, he votes in November. / If Carlos registers tonight, he will vote in November. / If Carlos will register tonight, he will vote in November.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  3. Ana tells her sister: If Carlos ___ (not pick up) a shift, he won't pay the bill on time.
    Answer / teacher checkdoesn't pick up,does not pick up

Unless, When, and As Soon As

It's Monday, October 19. Carlos is registered now. But Scott never saw his request sheet, and Carlos is on a double on Election Day, November 3 (7 to close). His coworker Miguel can't switch. So Carlos plans to vote early. This is his work week.

Unless = if not. Same tense rules as the First Conditional.
When = at that moment in the future (more certain than if).
As soon as = immediately when something happens.

unless = if not Carlos won't vote on Tuesday unless someone switches with him.
unless = if not Scott won't approve a day off unless you ask early.
when = certain future When Carlos finishes work on Friday, he will check the polling hours.
as soon as = immediately As soon as he votes on Saturday, he will text Ana a photo of his sticker.

Same rule: After unless, when, and as soon as, use present simple, not will.
Correct: As soon as he gets there, he will vote.
Wrong: As soon as he will get there, he will vote.

Read the week, then choose

Look at Carlos's week above. Choose the correct answer.

    If Carlos votes Saturday morning, he will still work Saturday night. / Carlos votes on Friday and works on Saturday morning. / Carlos doesn't work on Saturday.

    Answer / teacher checkb

    When the schedule posts, I'll text you. / As soon as the schedule will post, I'll text you. / I won't cover unless someone else steps up.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  4. Fill in: Ana won't go to the polls ___ her sister watches the kids. (When / Unless / As soon as)
    Answer / teacher checkunless,Unless

Zero vs. First: Which One Fits?

Miguel can't switch, so Carlos tells Scott his plan: vote early on Saturday morning. Scott says yes. He also tells Carlos a rule: Saturday nights at La Palma pay double. Carlos's plan and Scott's rule use two different conditionals. Look at the table.

Zero vs. First: side by side

Type Meaning Example
Zero
If + present, present 		Scott's rule. Always true. If you work Saturday nights, you earn double.
First
If + present, will + base 		Carlos's plan. A real future. If I vote Saturday morning, I will still work the night shift.

The key question: Is this always true (Zero) or is this one person's plan (First)?
"You earn double on Saturday nights" = always true at La Palma. Zero.
"I'll still work the night shift" = Carlos's plan for this Saturday. First.

    Answer / teacher checkb

    Answer / teacher checktakes

Beatriz lives downstairs. She is a citizen, but she doesn't drive. She cleans offices at night, and the polls close at 8.

Beatriz

Which type is each sentence?

first "If you're ready at 9, he'll pick you up." A real plan for tomorrow.
zero "My sister always says yes if I make her breakfast." Always true, every time.
first "If my sister comes for the kids, I can come with you." A real possibility for tomorrow.
as soon as "Call me as soon as you know." Same tense rule as First Conditional.

    AnswerIf I take the extra shift...

    In First Conditional, the if-part uses present simple. Never use 'will' in the if-part.

    If your name is on the list, you get a ballot. / If Carlos will work Saturday, he will pay the bill. / If I don't see you by 5, I will call you.

  3. Fill in the blank: "If you work Saturday nights, you ___ double pay." (Zero Conditional: Scott's always-true rule at La Palma.)

W8: Can, Should, Must

Weekly plan ·

Required lesson and practice

Can. What Your New Phone Can Do

Scene  East Boston Branch Library, tech help table. Tuesday, 4:30 PM, after work. Photo: Alfons Morales / Unsplash

Claudette's old phone broke last week. Her daughter Nadège lives in Haiti, and they talk every Sunday. Ryan at the library's tech help table sets up her new phone.

👨🏽
Ryan
Done. Your new phone is ready. You can call, text, and video-chat now.
👩🏾
Claudette
Can I video-call my daughter in Haiti? My old phone was too slow.
👨🏽
Ryan
Yes, you can. With WhatsApp and wifi, the call is free.
👩🏾
Claudette
I can't read these little letters. Can you make them bigger?
👨🏽
Ryan
Sure. And look, I saved Nadège's number. You can call her with one touch.
👩🏾
Claudette
Perfect. Now I can see her face every Sunday.

Can = ability or possibility. Something is possible, or a person is able to do it. Can't = it is not possible, or not able.

ability Claudette can video-call her daughter now.
possibility You can make the letters bigger in Settings.
not able She can't read the small letters.

Form: can + base verb (no -s, no -ing, no "to")
She can call her daughter.   Not: she can calls   Not: she can to call

Use can correctly

Choose the correct sentence or fill in the blank.

  1. Claudette wants to call her daughter. Which sentence is correct?

    She can calls Nadège on WhatsApp. / She can call Nadège on WhatsApp. / She can to call Nadège on WhatsApp.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  2. With wifi, Claudette ___ video-call Haiti for free.

    can / can't / must

    Answer / teacher checka
  3. Fill in: Claudette ___ (can / can't) read the small letters, so Ryan makes them bigger.
    Answer / teacher checkcan't,cannot

Build the sentence

Unscramble the words to make a correct sentence.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkRyan can make the letters bigger for you

Should. Advice From a Neighbor

On Wednesday night, Claudette gets a text from a new number:

"Hi Mom, it's me. I dropped my phone, so this is my new number. I need $200 for a new phone. Can you send it tonight?"

Claudette calls her neighbor Bruno. He writes her a list of advice. A ✅ means Claudette already did it.

Bruno's advice
What Claudette should do tonight
✅ She should call Nadège's old number first.
⬜ She should ask a question only Nadège knows.
⬜ She shouldn't send $200 tonight.
⬜ She shouldn't click any links in the text.

Should = advice or a recommendation. It is a good idea. Shouldn't = advice against something. It is not a good idea.

good idea You should call your daughter's old number first.
good idea You should ask a question only your family knows.
bad idea You shouldn't send money to a new number before you check.
bad idea You shouldn't click on links in texts from numbers you don't know.

Should is softer than must. It gives advice, not a rule. A friend, a neighbor, or a doctor might say should. A law or a bank's rule says must.

Good idea or bad idea?

Choose should or shouldn't to complete Bruno's advice.

  1. Look at Bruno's list. What has Claudette already done?

    She called Nadège's old number. / She asked about the old dog. / She sent $200.

    Answer / teacher checka
  2. Look at Bruno's list. Claudette ___ send $200 tonight.

    should / shouldn't / can't

    Answer / teacher checkb
  3. Claudette wants to check the text. Which advice is correct?

    She should calling her daughter on the old phone. / She should call her daughter on the old phone. / She should to call her daughter on the old phone.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  4. Look at Bruno's list. Claudette ___ (should / shouldn't) click any links in the text.
    Answer / teacher checkshouldn't,should not

Build the sentence

Unscramble the words to make a correct sentence.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkClaudette should ask about the old dog

Must and Must Not. Rules That Protect You

Claudette asked the new number about the old dog. It never answered. At 2 AM, one more text came: "Mom, just send me your card number and PIN." Before work, Claudette stops at her bank. Jessica at the front desk points to this notice.

Bank notice
Card safety rules
1 You must not share your PIN with anyone, not even family.
2 You must not give your card number to a stranger by text.
3 If you share your card number by mistake, you must call us right away.
4 You don't have to come to the bank. You can call the number on the back of your card.
We will NEVER ask for your PIN by text, email, or phone.

Must = strong obligation. It is required, not just a good idea. Must not (mustn't) = prohibition. It is not allowed. Do not do this.

required You must keep your PIN private.
required You must call the bank right away if someone has your card number.
not allowed You must not share your PIN with anyone, not even family.
not allowed You must not give your card number to a stranger by text.

Don't confuse must not and don't have to.
You must not share your PIN. = It is forbidden. Never do it.
You don't have to come to the bank. = It is not required. You can come in if you want, or you can call.

Required or forbidden?

Choose must or must not, and check your understanding.

  1. Look at the bank notice. You ___ share your PIN with anyone.

    must / must not / should

    Answer / teacher checkb
  2. Which sentence uses "must" correctly?

    You must to report the text to the bank. / You must reporting the text to the bank. / You must report the text to the bank.

    Answer / teacher checkc
  3. Look at the bank notice. Claudette has a cold and wants to stay home. Does she have to go to the bank?

    Yes. She must go to the bank. / No. She can call instead. / No. Going to the bank is forbidden.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  4. Look at the bank notice. You ___ give your card number to a stranger by text. (must / must not)
    Answer / teacher checkmust not,mustn't

Build the sentence

Unscramble the words to make a correct sentence.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkYou must not text your card number to anyone

Putting It Together. Which Modal Fits?

Scene  Evening ESOL class, Thursday. Ms. Tran asks Claudette to tell the class her story. Photo: Kenny Eliason / Unsplash
👩🏻
Ms. Tran
Claudette, you got a strange text this week. Can you tell the class?
👩🏾
Claudette
A "new number" said it was my daughter. It asked for $200, then my PIN.
👩🏻
Ms. Tran
That's a common scam. What should people do?
👩🏾
Claudette
You shouldn't send anything. You should call the real number. And you must never share your PIN.
👩🏻
Ms. Tran
And did you reach Nadège?
👩🏾
Claudette
Yes! This morning she video-called me. Her phone was fine the whole time. She never sent that text.

The three modals side by side:

Modal Meaning and example
can / can't ability or possibility
Scammers can pretend to be your family.
should / shouldn't advice, recommendation
You should call the real number.
must / must not strong rule, prohibition
You must not share your PIN.

All three modals use the same form: modal + base verb (no -s, no -ing, no "to").
She can call her.   You should check it.   He must report it.

Want to go deeper?: This was the quick version. If you want more examples, more exercises, and the full explanation, open the Modals: Obligation + Permission Full Guide (app reference).

    Modal verbs (can, should, must) are always followed by the base verb with no changes.

  2. Which sentence has an error?

W9: Have You Ever...?

Weekly plan ·

Required lesson and practice

Catching Up on the Phone

Scene  East Boston, Tuesday evening, a month before Jean's visit. Claudette texts her cousin Jean in Montreal. Photo: Jonas Leupe / Unsplash
👩🏾
Claudette
You’re visiting next month, right? Have you ever helped at a food pantry?
👨🏽
Jean
Yes, I have. I packed boxes at my church in Montreal last winter. Why?
👩🏾
Claudette
The pantry near Maverick Square needs volunteers that Saturday. A lot of the families there speak Creole.
👨🏽
Jean
Good, we can translate. Have you ever volunteered there?
👩🏾
Claudette
No, I haven’t. But I picked up food there when I first came. They were kind to me.
👨🏽
Jean
Then sign us both up. Send me the time and the address.

Have you ever...? = Did this happen at any time in your life? We do not say when. We just want to know: yes or no, has this experience happened to you?

any time Have you ever eaten a tamale? (in your whole life)
any time Have you ever been to a city council meeting?
any time Have you ever volunteered in your community?

The form: Have + subject + ever + V3 (past participle)
Example: Have you ever eaten / been / taken / tried

Timeline labels: Have you ever...? (past)

What does it mean?

Choose the best meaning for each question.

  1. "Have you ever taken an English class before?"

    Did you take a class last week? / Are you in a class right now? / At any time in your life, did you take a class?

    Answer / teacher checkc
  2. "Have you ever visited the East Boston library?"

    Do you go to the library every week? / Did this happen at any point in your life? / Are you at the library right now?

    Answer / teacher checkb

Build the question

Unscramble the words to make a correct "Have you ever" question.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkHave you ever visited city hall
  2. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkHave you ever called 311 about a problem

Write the missing word

Fill in the blank with the correct form.

  1. Have you ever ___ (be) to a community meeting in East Boston?
    Answer / teacher checkbeen
  2. Have you ever ___ (ride) the Blue Line to the airport?
    Answer / teacher checkridden

Did you go? vs. Have you been?

Three weeks later, after class. Amara shows Claudette her list of things she did in East Boston. Look at the list. Some things she did at a specific time. Some things she has never done.

Amara's list
East Boston: what Amara has done
✅ Pantry: went last Saturday
✅ Library: took a class in 2023
✅ Health clinic: visited in March
⬜ City hall: has never been
⬜ 311: has never called
Past Simple
Did you go to the festival?
Specific time. We know when: last Saturday, yesterday, in 2022.
Present Perfect
Have you ever been to a festival?
Any time in your life. No specific time needed.
specific time Did you call 311 last week?
any time Have you ever called 311?
specific time Did you go to the food pantry in March?
any time Have you ever been to the food pantry?

Key rule: If the question includes a specific time (last Saturday, yesterday, in 2020), use Past Simple. If there is no time, or you say "ever," use Have you...?

You will also hear "Did you ever...?" for life experience, especially in American English. It is OK. In this lesson, practice "Have you ever...?"

Timeline labels: Did you go? (specific time) (past) → Have you been? (any time) (past)

Which question fits?

Choose the correct question for each situation.

  1. Look at Amara's list. Which sentence is true?

    Amara has been to the health clinic. / Amara has called 311. / Amara has visited city hall.

    Answer / teacher checka
  2. Amara's list says she took a library class in 2023. Which question asks about that exact year?

    Did you take a class at the library in 2023? / Have you ever taken a class at the library?

    Answer / teacher checka
  3. You want to know if your classmate went to a cultural event at any point in her life.

    Did you go to a cultural event last year? / Have you ever been to a cultural event?

    Answer / teacher checkb
  4. You know there was a free legal clinic last Thursday. You want to know if your neighbor went.

    Did you go to the legal clinic last Thursday? / Have you ever been to a legal clinic?

    Answer / teacher checka
  5. You want to know if your coworker has experience donating blood at any point in his life.

    Did you donate blood last summer? / Have you ever donated blood?

    Answer / teacher checkb

Correct or not correct?

Is the underlined question correct for the situation described?

  1. Situation: You are asking about last weekend specifically. Question: "<strong>Have you tried Guatemalan food last weekend?</strong>"

    Correct / Not correct. Should be 'Did you try Guatemalan food last weekend?'

    Answer / teacher checkincorrect
  2. Situation: You are asking about last week specifically. Question: "<strong>Did you go to the community meeting last Tuesday?</strong>"

    Correct / Not correct. Should use Have you ever.

    Answer / teacher checkcorrect

Fill in the blank

Write the correct verb form.

  1. Look at Amara's list. Has Amara ever called 311? Write the short answer: "No, she ___."
    Answer / teacher checkhasn't,has not
  2. Have you ever ___ (see) a free concert in Boston?
    Answer / teacher checkseen
  3. ___ you go to the school orientation last September? (Did / Have)
    Answer / teacher checkDid

Yes, I have. No, I haven't.

Scene  East Boston Community Center, Wednesday, 6 PM, a month later. Jean arrived from Montreal on Monday. He and Claudette come to the volunteer orientation. Kevin, the pantry coordinator, meets the new volunteers. Photo: Headway / Unsplash
🧑🏻
Kevin
Welcome, Jean. Have you ever volunteered at a food pantry before?
👨🏽
Jean
Yes, I have. I packed boxes at my church in Montreal last winter.
🧑🏻
Kevin
Great. And Claudette, have you ever done any food distribution work?
👩🏾
Claudette
No, I haven't. But I got food here when I first came. I want to help back.

Short answers: Always use have or haven't in your reply. Do not just say "yes" or "no."

yes Yes, I have. (Then add details with past simple: "I worked there in 2019.")
no No, I haven't. (You can add: "But I would like to try.")

After "Yes, I have" use Past Simple for the details:

"Have you ever used the food pantry?"
"Yes, I have. I went there last winter."

example "Have you ever taken a citizenship class?" / "Yes, I have. I took one at Bunker Hill two years ago."
example "Have you ever called 311?" / "No, I haven't. What is it for?"

Choose the correct short answer

Pick the best reply to each question.

  1. "Have you ever volunteered at a school?" (She has, in 2022.)

    Yes, I volunteered. / Yes, I have. I helped at an elementary school in 2022. / Yes, I was volunteering.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  2. "Have you ever used the MBTA app?" (He hasn't.)

    No, I didn't. / No, I don't. / No, I haven't.

    Answer / teacher checkc

Build the answer

Unscramble the words to make a correct short answer with a detail.

  1. Unscramble: (answering yes, with a detail about last year)
    Answer / teacher checkYes, I have. I went to a health fair last year.

Write the reply

Fill in the blank to complete the short answer.

  1. "Have you ever been to a community garden?" "Yes, I ___."
    Answer / teacher checkhave
  2. "Have you ever called your city councilor?" "No, I ___."
    Answer / teacher checkhaven't

Real Practice: Your Community

Saturday morning. Before their first shift, Claudette and Jean read about a man who feeds people in a crisis. Notice how the reading says what he has done, then gives details in the past.

Famous person
José Andrés: A Cook Who Feeds Communities

José Andrés was born in Spain. In the early 1990s, he moved to the United States. He arrived in New York City at age 21. In 2013, he became a U.S. citizen.

He has worked as a chef in restaurants, but he has also helped many people in a crisis. His group, World Central Kitchen, has served chef-prepared meals to communities after natural disasters. It has helped people in places like Guam, Panama, and Ukraine.

Photo: U.S. Department of State, public domain. Sources: World Central Kitchen, The Washington Post (2013), Wikipedia: José Andrés

Common East Boston community questions:

  • Have you ever taken the Blue Line?
  • Have you ever been to a free health clinic?
  • Have you ever used the food pantry on Maverick Street?
  • Have you ever signed a petition?
  • Have you ever attended an ESL class before this one?
  • Have you ever called 311 to report a problem?

    Answer / teacher checkb

Past Simple or Present Perfect?

Choose the correct tense for each sentence.

    Answer / teacher checkmoved

Build a question

Unscramble to make a correct question.

    Answer / teacher checkHave you ever signed a petition in East Boston
  2. Unscramble:

  2. In what year did José Andrés become a U.S. citizen?

Guide mini-quiz

  1. Your neighbor wants to know if you have any experience with the night class, at any time in your life. Which question should she ask?

    Did you go to the night class last week? / Have you ever taken the night class? / Do you take the night class?

    AnswerHave you ever taken the night class?

    Have you ever is for life experience with no specific time.

  2. Fill in the blank: "Have you ever ___ to a city council meeting?" (V3 of 'be')
    Answerbeen

    After 'have you ever', always use V3. The V3 of 'be' is 'been'.

  3. "Have you ever called 311?" Claudette says no. What is the best reply?

    No, I didn't. / No, I haven't. / No, I don't.

    AnswerNo, I haven't.

    Short answer for Have you ever uses haven't (not didn't or don't).

  4. Build the question by tapping the words in order.
    AnswerHave you ever applied for a library card

    Have you ever + V3 asks about life experience with no specific time.

  5. Jean says: "I have went to a food pantry two years ago." What is wrong?

    Should be: I went to a food pantry two years ago. (specific time needs Past Simple) / Should be: I have gone to a food pantry two years ago. / Nothing is wrong.

    AnswerShould be: I went to a food pantry two years ago. (specific time needs Past Simple)

    Two years ago is a specific time, so Past Simple is required. Never use present perfect with a finished time expression.

W10: What Are You Good At?

Weekly plan ·

Required lesson and practice

Before the Dinner Rush

Scene  East Boston, Thursday, 4 PM. Diego and Sarah prep in the kitchen before the dinner rush. Photo: Filipp Romanovski / Unsplash

On Monday, a car almost hit a boy at the crosswalk on Saratoga Street, right by the school. Tonight at 7, the neighbors are having a meeting about it at the library. Diego is a line cook. His shift ends at 6:30, if the kitchen isn't too busy.

👩🏻
Sarah
Are you going to the crosswalk meeting tonight? They need people to sign up for jobs.
👨🏽
Diego
I have to. My son crosses there every day. I'm afraid of letting him go alone now.
👩🏻
Sarah
So what are you going to sign up for? What are you good at?
👨🏽
Diego
I'm good at cooking fast. I don't think that fixes traffic.
👩🏻
Sarah
Bring food. People stay longer when there's food.
👨🏽
Diego
Ha. OK, but I'm more interested in getting a traffic light.

The pattern: adjective + preposition + verb-ing

After words like good at, interested in, and afraid of, the next verb ends in -ing. This is called a gerund.

adjective + at I'm good at cooking fast.
adjective + in I'm interested in getting a traffic light.
adjective + of I'm afraid of letting him go alone.
Common pairs to learn:
  • good at + -ing
  • bad at + -ing
  • interested in + -ing
  • afraid of + -ing
  • tired of + -ing
  • worried about + -ing

Exercise 1: Choose the correct preposition

Pick the word that completes the sentence correctly.

  1. Diego is good ___ cooking fast.

    at / in / of

    Answer / teacher checkat
  2. Diego is interested ___ getting a traffic light.

    at / in / of

    Answer / teacher checkin
  3. Diego is afraid ___ letting his son cross alone.

    at / in / of

    Answer / teacher checkof
  4. "I am good at cook." Is this sentence correct?

    Correct / Not correct. Should be 'good at cooking'

    Answer / teacher checkincorrect

Exercise 2: Complete the sentence

Type the correct -ing form of the verb.

  1. Sarah is good at ___ (chop) onions quickly.
    Answer / teacher checkchopping
  2. Diego is interested in ___ (learn) who to call at City Hall.
    Answer / teacher checklearning

Outside the Meeting

Thursday, 7:15 PM, inside the library. The meeting has started. Marta cleans rooms at a hotel. Bruno paints houses. The first idea is a morning crossing watch: neighbors in orange vests help kids cross from 7:30 to 8:00. Bruno signs up for Tuesdays. Marta takes Thursdays. Ms. Patel asks everyone how they feel and writes it down.

Neighbor survey
How do you feel about the crossing watch?
Neighbor Feeling About
Marta tired of looking for a safe place to cross
Bruno nervous about working the corner alone
Bruno's daughter excited about seeing him in a vest
The neighbors proud of starting the crossing watch

Look at the Feeling column. Every feeling has a preposition (of, about), and the next verb ends in -ing.

Look at the Neighbor survey. Pick the best answer.

    Marta / Bruno / Bruno's daughter

    Answer / teacher checkbruno
  2. The neighbors are ___ starting the crossing watch.

    tired of / proud of / nervous about

    Answer / teacher checkproud

    Marta is nervous about helping the kids. / Bruno's daughter is excited about seeing her dad at the corner. / Bruno is proud of finding a safe place to cross.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  4. "She is excited about start the crossing watch." Is this correct?

    Correct / Not correct. Should be 'excited about starting'

    Answer / teacher checkincorrect

Put the words in the correct order.

    Answer / teacher checkShe is nervous about driving in snow
  2. Unscramble:

Type the correct -ing form of the verb.

  1. My son is excited about ___ (ride) the school bus.
    Answer / teacher checkriding

    Answer / teacher checkstanding

Suggestions for the City

Ms. Patel runs the neighborhood group. Next Tuesday, she takes a letter to the city's traffic office. Diego comes in late, still in his kitchen shoes, with a tray of empanadas. Ms. Patel writes the plan on the board.

On the board
Ms. Patel's plan for the letter
1 Thank people for coming to the meeting.
2 Show the city the problem by sending photos of cars that don't stop.
3 Ask about getting a morning crossing guard.
4 Don't leave without signing the letter.
Diego takes the photos. He walks his son to school there every day.

Look at the bold words in the plan. for, by, about, and without are prepositions too. Same rule: preposition + -ing.

Exercise 1: Read the plan

Look at Ms. Patel's plan on the board. Pick the best answer.

  1. How does the group show the city the problem?

    By sending photos / By writing a song / By waiting a year

    Answer / teacher checka
  2. What should people NOT do?

    Go home without writing their name / Thank people for coming / Ask about a crossing guard

    Answer / teacher checka
  3. Marta got a seat in the front by ___ early.

    arriving / arrive / arrived

    Answer / teacher checkarriving
  4. Don't sign the letter without ___ it first.

    reading / read / to read

    Answer / teacher checkreading

Exercise 2: Complete the sentence

Type the correct -ing form of the verb in parentheses.

  1. Ms. Patel says, "The city listens to us. We get results by ___ (show) up every time."
    Answer / teacher checkshowing
  2. Diego helps the group by ___ (bring) food.
    Answer / teacher checkbringing

The Sign-Up Card

Scene  Thursday, 8:15 PM, the front desk of Room B. Amina fills out a sign-up card on a clipboard. Photo: Scott Graham / Unsplash

Before people leave, Kevin hands out sign-up cards. The card asks two questions: What are you good at? What are you interested in doing? Amina is a home health aide. Her shift starts at 6 tomorrow morning.

🧑🏻
Kevin
This card asks what you're good at. Just write two or three things.
👩🏿
Amina
I'm good at translating. Somali and Arabic. Does that help?
🧑🏻
Kevin
A lot. Half the families on that street can't read the letter in English.
👩🏿
Amina
I can do it, but I'm worried about finishing tonight. I work at six.
🧑🏻
Kevin
Take it home. Bring it back Monday. The letter goes to the city Tuesday.

Two weeks later: The letter goes to the city with 214 names, in English, Spanish, Somali and Arabic. The city puts a flashing light at the Saratoga Street crosswalk. Diego's son walks to school by himself again. On Tuesdays, Bruno is at the corner in his orange vest.

All the patterns together. The pattern is always the same: preposition + verb-ing.

Quick review:
  • I am good at translating.
  • Diego is interested in getting a traffic light.
  • Marta is tired of looking for a safe place to cross.
  • Amina is worried about finishing tonight.
  • Thank you for com ing.
  • Don't leave without sign ing the letter.

Guide mini-quiz

  1. Diego says, 'I am good ___ cooking fast.' Which word fits?

    at / in / of

    Answerat

    Good at + -ing is the fixed pattern. 'Good in' and 'good of' are not used this way.

  2. Marta says, 'I am tired of look for a safe place to cross.' What is wrong?

    Nothing is wrong. / 'look' should be 'looking'. A verb after a preposition needs -ing. / 'of' should be 'for'.

    Answer'look' should be 'looking'. A verb after a preposition needs -ing.

    After a preposition like 'of', the verb must be in -ing form: tired of looking.

  3. Fill in the blank: "Amina is interested ___ translating the letter." (Which preposition pairs with 'interested'?)
    Answerin

    The fixed phrase is 'interested in'. Always followed by -ing.

  4. Sarah asks Diego what he is good at. Put the words in order.
    AnswerI am good at cooking fast

    Good at + -ing. The verb after 'at' must end in -ing.

  5. Which sentence is correct?

    Don't sign without read the letter. / Don't sign without reading the letter. / Don't sign without to read the letter.

    AnswerDon't sign without reading the letter.

    'Without' is a preposition. The verb after it must be -ing: without reading.

W11: How Long + For and Since

Weekly plan ·

Required lesson and practice

How Long Have You Been Here?

Scene  Hotel laundry room, East Boston. Tuesday morning, before the shift starts. Photo: Oli Woodman / Unsplash

Yesenia works in the laundry room of a hotel in East Boston. This week she moved to the morning shift, so she is meeting new coworkers. Claudette is a housekeeper. She brings a cart of towels to the laundry room.

👩🏽
Yesenia
How long have you worked here?
👩🏾
Claudette
I have worked here for five years. I started in the laundry, then moved to housekeeping.
👩🏽
Yesenia
How long have you been in Boston?
👩🏾
Claudette
I have been here since 2020. You?
👩🏽
Yesenia
I have lived in East Boston for five years.

For / Since with present perfect = the situation started in the past and is still true right now. Claudette still works there. Yesenia still lives in East Boston.

for I have worked here for five years.
since I have been in Boston since 2020.
for Yesenia has lived in East Boston for five years.

The form: Subject + have / has + V3 + for or since + time
Examples: have worked, have been, has lived, have had, has known

Timeline labels: have worked / have lived (past)

What does it mean?

Choose the best meaning for each sentence.

  1. "Claudette has worked at the hotel for five years."

    She worked there a long time ago but stopped. / She started five years ago and still works there now. / She is going to work there for two years.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  2. "I have lived in East Boston since 2020."

    I moved away from East Boston in 2020. / I lived in East Boston in 2020 but not now. / I moved to East Boston in 2020 and I still live here.

    Answer / teacher checkc

Build the sentence

Unscramble the words to make a correct sentence.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkClaudette has been in Boston since 2020
  2. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkI have worked at this hotel since 2024

Write the missing word

Fill in the blank with the correct form of the verb.

  1. She ___ (work) at the hotel for two years.
    Answer / teacher checkhas worked
  2. We ___ (live) in this apartment since 2021.
    Answer / teacher checkhave lived

For vs. Since: What's the Difference?

It is October 2026. Later on Tuesday, Yesenia comes home from work and finds a letter from her landlord in the mailbox. The landlord is not renewing leases in the spring. Look at Yesenia's years in East Boston.

Timeline
Yesenia in East Boston
2021
The family moves into the apartment. Since 2021 is the starting point.
for five years
Oct 2026
Today. The letter from the landlord arrives. Yesenia has lived here for five years.
For = the whole bar (a length of time). Since = where the bar starts (a starting point).
For
A length of time
for 4 years, for 6 months, for a long time, for 3 days
Since
A starting point
since 2020, since March, since I moved here, since my son was born
for I have lived here for five years. (= a length of time)
since I have lived here since 2021. (= a starting point)
for She has had the same phone company for three years.
since She has had the same job since 2024.

For or Since?

Choose the correct word for each blank.

  1. Yesenia's family has lived in that apartment ___ five years.

    for (length of time) / since (starting point)

    Answer / teacher checkfor
  2. Look at the timeline. Which sentence is true?

    Yesenia has lived in East Boston since five years. / Yesenia has lived in East Boston since 2021. / Yesenia has lived in East Boston for 2021.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  3. They have looked for a new apartment ___ October.

    for (length of time) / since (starting point)

    Answer / teacher checksince
  4. Claudette has worked at the hotel ___ five years.

    for (length of time) / since (starting point)

    Answer / teacher checkfor

Correct or not correct?

Is the underlined word correct?

  1. "I have worked here <strong>since</strong> three years."

    Correct / Not correct. Should be 'for three years' (three years is a length, not a starting point)

    Answer / teacher checkincorrect
  2. "She has been in Boston <strong>since</strong> 2019."

    Correct / Not correct. Should be 'for 2019'

    Answer / teacher checkcorrect

Fill in the blank

Write 'for' or 'since'.

  1. I have had this apartment ___ March.
    Answer / teacher checksince
  2. She has worked at the laundry ___ two years.
    Answer / teacher checkfor

The landlord's letter asks every tenant to fill out a move-out form. Kevin in the leasing office gives Yesenia the form. 🏠 Home East Boston apartment 2021
🧺 Job Hotel laundry room 2024
📱 Phone Same company. New plan: $40 (was $65). 2023

Kevin reads the form and asks questions with How long...?

How long have you...? is the question. The answer uses for or since.

The question pattern:

How long + have/has + subject + V3?
How long have you had this plan?
How long has she worked here?
How long have they lived in that building?

question How long have you lived in East Boston?
answer I have lived here for five years. / Since 2021.
question How long has your sister had that job?
answer She has had it since March.

Timeline labels: How long have you had...? (past)

Choose the correct answer

Pick the best reply to each question.

  1. "How long have you had your winter jacket?"

    I had this jacket for two winters ago. / I have had this jacket for two winters. / I have had this jacket two winters ago.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  2. Look at Yesenia's form. Kevin asks: "How long has Yesenia worked at the hotel?"

    She has worked there since two years. / She has worked there for 2024. / She has worked there for two years.

    Answer / teacher checkc

Build the question

Unscramble to make a correct 'How long' question.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkHow long have you had this phone plan
  2. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkHow long has she worked at the hotel

Write the missing verb

Fill in the blank with the correct form of the verb in parentheses.

  1. How long ___ you ___ (have) that job?
    Answer / teacher checkhave had
  2. Look at the form. Yesenia ___ (have) the same phone company since 2023.
    Answer / teacher checkhas had

For and Since on the Timeline

Some things are finished. Some things are still true now. Read about Luis von Ahn. Which verbs are finished? Which verbs are still true now?

Real person
Luis von Ahn

Luis von Ahn was born in Guatemala City, Guatemala. He came to the United States at 18 to study math at Duke University. He finished his degree in 2000. In 2009, he sold a website security tool called reCAPTCHA to Google.

In 2011, he and Severin Hacker started Duolingo, an app for learning languages. Von Ahn has worked on Duolingo since then, and he is still its CEO today.

Photo: Jarek Tuszyński, 2015, CC BY 4.0. Sources: Carnegie Corporation of New York, National Inventors Hall of Fame, Lemelson-MIT
Present Perfect + For / Since
I have worked here for two years.
Started in the past. Still true NOW.
Past Simple
I took a day off last month.
Finished. Done. A specific time in the past.

Key question to ask yourself: Is this situation still true NOW? Use present perfect + for/since. Is it finished? Use past simple.

still true now Her family has had the same apartment for five years.
finished They moved into that apartment in 2021.
still true now He has known the manager since he started.
finished He met the manager on his first day.

Timeline labels: has worked (still true now) (past) → worked (finished) (past)

Still true now or finished?

Choose the correct tense for each sentence.

  1. Read about Luis von Ahn. In 2009, he ___ reCAPTCHA to Google.

    sold / has sold

    Answer / teacher checksold
  2. Read about Luis von Ahn. He ___ on Duolingo since 2011. (He still works on it.)

    worked / has worked

    Answer / teacher checkhas worked
  3. Yesenia ___ at the hotel for two years. (She still works there.)

    worked / has worked

    Answer / teacher checkhas worked

Error correction

One sentence uses the wrong tense. Choose the correct version.

  1. "I have worked here for two years ago."

    Correct as is. / I worked here two years ago. (finished action needs past simple) / I have worked here for two years. (no 'ago' with present perfect)

    Answer / teacher checkc

Fill in the blank

Write the correct form of the verb in parentheses.

  1. Claudette ___ (work) at the hotel for five years. She still works there.
    Answer / teacher checkhas worked
  2. Read about Luis von Ahn. He ___ (finish) his degree at Duke in 2000.
    Answer / teacher checkfinished

Real Practice: Lease, Job, and Family

Scene  Yesenia's apartment, East Boston. Sunday dinner, three weeks later. Photo: Nicole Michalou / Unsplash

Yesenia is saving money with her cheaper phone plan. She found an apartment nearby, and the new landlord sent a rental application. On Sunday, Yesenia, her mother Lupe, and her little brother Mateo sit down to dinner. After dinner, Yesenia and Lupe fill out the form.

👩🏽
Yesenia
Mami, this rental application asks how long we have lived here. Five years, right?
👩🏾
Lupe
Yes, we have lived here for five years. Since Mateo was in kindergarten.
👩🏽
Yesenia
Our lease ends in March, and everything nearby costs more.
👩🏾
Lupe
Mateo has gone to that school since kindergarten. I don't want to change his school.
👩🏽
Yesenia
Neither do I. This apartment is close to his school. I have been looking at apartments nearby for weeks.

Common real-life situations that use for and since:

  • I have lived here for five years.
  • I have worked this shift since October.
  • She has had the same phone company for three years.
  • We have known our landlord since we moved in.
  • How long has it been since you saw your family?

Want to go deeper?: This was the quick version. For more examples, more exercises, and the full explanation of all present perfect uses, open the Present Perfect Full Guide (app reference).

For or Since?

Choose the correct word to complete each sentence.

  1. Yesenia's family has lived in the apartment ___ five years.

    for / since

    Answer / teacher checkfor
  2. Yesenia has had the same phone company ___ 2023. (She wrote it on her move-out form.)

    for / since

    Answer / teacher checksince
  3. Yesenia's brother Mateo has gone to the same school ___ kindergarten.

    for / since

    Answer / teacher checksince

Build the sentence

Unscramble to make a correct sentence.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkWe have lived in this apartment for five years
  2. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkHow long has it been since you called your brother

Error correction

Find the mistake and choose the correct sentence.

  1. "She has lived here since five years."

    Correct as is. / She has lived here for five years. ('five years' is a length, not a starting point) / She lived here for five years.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  2. "I have worked here for 2021."

    Correct as is. / I have worked here since 2021. ('2021' is a starting point, not a length) / I worked here since 2021.

    Answer / teacher checkb

Fill in the blank

Write the correct form of the verb in parentheses.

  1. Yesenia ___ (work) in the hotel laundry for two years.
    Answer / teacher checkhas worked
  2. How long ___ they ___ (know) their landlord?
    Answer / teacher checkhave known

Guide mini-quiz

  1. Yesenia chose her phone company three years ago, in 2023. She wants to say how long she has had it, using 'for'. What does she say?

    I have had this company for since three years. / I have had this company for three years. / I have had this company for 2023.

    AnswerI have had this company for three years.

    'For' takes a length of time (three years), not a starting year (2023).

  2. Yesenia's friend asks about her apartment. Choose the correct for/since sentence.

    She has lived here since five years. / She has lived here for 2021. / She has lived here since 2021.

    AnswerShe has lived here since 2021.

    'Since' goes with a starting point like a year or date. 'For' goes with a length of time like 'four years'.

  3. Fill in the blank: "I have lived here ___ 2020." (Which word shows a starting point in time?)
    Answersince

    'Since' goes with a specific starting point (a year, a date, a moment). 'For' goes with a length of time.

  4. Your neighbor asks how long you have lived in East Boston. Put the words in order.
    AnswerHow long have you lived here

    For ongoing duration questions, use 'How long have/has + subject + past participle?'

  5. Luis von Ahn sold reCAPTCHA to Google in 2009. He does not own reCAPTCHA now. Which sentence is correct?

    He has sold reCAPTCHA since 2009. / He has sold reCAPTCHA for 2009. / He sold reCAPTCHA to Google in 2009.

    AnswerHe sold reCAPTCHA to Google in 2009.

    A finished action with a specific past time (2009) needs past simple, not present perfect.

W12: More, Less, the Most: Comparatives + Superlatives

Weekly plan ·

Required lesson and practice

Which One Is Cheaper?

After work, Rosa and her friend Amara compare two stores. Rosa saved her receipts. Look at the example prices.

Rosa's receipts Market Basket Dollar store
Beans $1.20 $1.80
Oil $5.00 $3.50
Walk 8 min 15 min

Beans are cheaper at Market Basket. The oil is more expensive there. The walk is shorter.

Comparatives compare two things. Use them with than: Market Basket is cheaper than the dollar store.

Short adjectives
cheap +er = cheaper
short +er = shorter
big +ger = bigger
close +r = closer
Long adjectives
more expensive
more convenient
more affordable
more reliable

Irregular comparatives

good better  |  bad worse  |  far farther / further

short The walk is shorter than I thought.
long The oil is more expensive here than at the dollar store.
irregular The rice is better quality here.

Comparative or not?

Choose the correct comparative form.

  1. Look at Rosa's receipts. Market Basket is ___ than the dollar store for beans. (cheap)

    more cheap / cheaper / cheapest

    Answer / teacher checkcheaper
  2. Look at Rosa's receipts. The oil at the dollar store is ___ than the oil at Market Basket. (affordable)

    affordabler / more affordabler / more affordable

    Answer / teacher checkmore affordable
  3. Look at Rosa's receipts. The walk to Market Basket is ___ than the walk to the dollar store. (short)

    more short / shorter / shortest

    Answer / teacher checkshorter
  4. The quality of this bread is ___ than the other brand. (good)

    gooder / more good / better

    Answer / teacher checkbetter

Build the comparison

Unscramble the words to make a correct sentence.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkThe oil is cheaper at the dollar store
  2. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkThe walk to Market Basket is shorter

Write the comparative

Fill in the blank with the comparative form of the adjective.

  1. Look at Rosa's receipts. How many minutes longer is the walk to the dollar store? Write a number.
    Answer / teacher check7
  2. The dollar store is ___ (far) from my apartment than Market Basket.
    Answer / teacher checkfarther,further
  3. The bus is ___ (slow) than walking from the stop.
    Answer / teacher checkslower

The Cheapest Plan I Could Find

Scene  Phone store on Meridian Street. Rosa compares three prepaid plans. Photo: Tyler Lastovich / Unsplash
🧑🏻
Kevin
I have three plans here. Which one do you want?
👩🏽
Rosa
Which one is the cheapest?
🧑🏻
Kevin
Plan C. It is the least expensive at $35 a month.
👩🏽
Rosa
And which one has the most data?
🧑🏻
Kevin
Plan B. But Plan C is the best value for the price.
👩🏽
Rosa
Then Plan C. I don’t need the most data. I need the cheapest bill.

Superlatives compare three or more things and name the one at the top (or bottom). Always use the before a superlative.

Short adjectives
cheap the cheapest
short the shortest
big the biggest
close the closest
Long adjectives
the most expensive
the most convenient
the least expensive
the most reliable

Irregular superlatives

good the best  |  bad the worst  |  far the farthest / furthest

short Plan C is the cheapest option.
long Plan A is the most expensive of the three.
irregular Plan C is the best value for the price.

Comparative or superlative?

Choose the correct form for each sentence.

  1. Of the three plans, Plan C is ___. (cheap)

    cheaper (comparative) / the cheapest (superlative) / most cheap

    Answer / teacher checkthe cheapest
  2. Plan B is ___ than Plan C for data. (expensive)

    the most expensive (superlative) / more expensive (comparative) / expensiver

    Answer / teacher checkmore expensive
  3. Which plan is ___? (good)

    gooder / better / the best

    Answer / teacher checkthe best

Error correction

Find the mistake and choose the correct sentence.

  1. "Plan C is most cheapest of all."

    Correct as is. / Plan C is the most cheapest of all. / Plan C is the cheapest of all. (short adjective: just add -est, no 'most')

    Answer / teacher checkc
  2. "This plan is the more convenient for my schedule."

    Correct as is. / This plan is the most convenient for my schedule. (superlative needs 'most', not 'more') / This plan is convenientest for my schedule.

    Answer / teacher checkb

Write the superlative

Fill in the blank with the superlative form.

  1. Plan A is ___ (expensive) of the three options.
    Answer / teacher checkthe most expensive
  2. Rosa chose Plan C because it is ___ (good) deal for the price.
    Answer / teacher checkthe best

More Rooms, Less Rent

Rosa's friends Fernanda and Diego need a new apartment. They look at three listings. The bars show the rent.

Listings
Rent, bedrooms, and trip to work
Bremen St $1,800
a month 3 bedrooms | 40 minutes to work
Maverick St $1,600
a month 2 bedrooms | 30 minutes to work
Chelsea St $1,300
a month 1 bedroom | 20 minutes to work

Use more for both countable and uncountable things. Use less for uncountable things. Use fewer for countable things you can count one by one.

Less (you cannot count it)
less noise
less rent
less space
less traffic
Fewer (you can count them)
fewer closets
fewer rooms
fewer problems
fewer neighbors
more This apartment has more rooms than our old one.
less Chelsea Street costs less money than Bremen Street.
fewer We want fewer problems with the landlord.

Less or fewer?

Choose the correct word for each blank.

  1. Look at the listings. The Chelsea Street apartment has ___ bedrooms than the Maverick Street apartment.

    less / fewer

    Answer / teacher checkfewer
  2. Look at the listings. The Chelsea Street apartment costs ___ money than the Bremen Street apartment.

    less / fewer

    Answer / teacher checkless
  3. Look at the listings. The trip from Maverick Street takes ___ time than the trip from Bremen Street.

    less / fewer

    Answer / teacher checkless
  4. Diego wants ___ problems with the landlord than last time.

    less / fewer

    Answer / teacher checkfewer

Build the sentence

Unscramble the words to make a correct sentence.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkChelsea Street costs less than Bremen Street
  2. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkWe need fewer boxes in the hallway

Fill in the blank

Write 'more', 'less', or 'fewer'.

  1. Look at the rent bars. Bremen Street costs $___ more a month than Maverick Street. Write a number.
    Answer / teacher check200,$200
  2. Write more, less, or fewer. Maverick Street takes ___ minutes to get to work than Bremen Street.
    Answer / teacher checkfewer
  3. We want ___ repairs this winter. (things you can count)
    Answer / teacher checkfewer

The Best Deal This Week

Scene  Flower stall near St. Mary's, East Boston. Saturday morning. Photo: Kelvin Zyteng / Unsplash
👩🏽
Rosa
I need marigolds for my window box. They’re more expensive than last year.
🧑🏾
Vendor
Yes, but these are the freshest on the street. Look at the color.
👩🏽
Rosa
The shop on Sumner has the lowest price. But it is farther.
🧑🏾
Vendor
Buy here and save the bus fare. It is the better deal today.
👩🏽
Rosa
All right. I’ll take two bundles, please.

Comparison language appears everywhere: store signs, apartment ads, phone plans, and conversations. The same rules apply: -er / more for two things, -est / the most for three or more.

Comparison language in real life

  • better than / worse than (comparing two things)
  • the best / the worst (of all options)
  • the most + adjective / the least + adjective
  • more + noun / less + uncountable / fewer + countable
ad language "The freshest flowers on the block."
listing "The cheapest 2BR apartment near the 116 bus. More space, less rent."
conversation "It costs more here but the quality is better."

Want to go deeper?: This was the quick version. For more examples, more exercises, and the full explanation of comparatives, superlatives, and quantifiers, open the Comparatives + Superlatives + Quantifiers Full Guide (app reference).

Reading real comparisons

Choose the correct meaning for each sentence.

  1. "The flowers here are the freshest on the street."

    The flowers are fresher than one other shop. / The flowers are fresher than all other shops on the street. / The flowers were fresh yesterday.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  2. "This apartment is the cheapest 2BR near the 116 bus."

    This apartment is cheaper than one other apartment. / This apartment costs less than all other 2BRs near the 116 bus. / This apartment was cheap last year.

    Answer / teacher checkb

Comparative or superlative?

Choose the correct form for each blank.

  1. Of all the flower stalls on the street, this one has ___ prices. (low)

    lower (comparative. 2 things) / the lowest (superlative. all stalls)

    Answer / teacher checkthe lowest
  2. The Sumner shop is ___ than this stall. (far)

    the farthest (superlative) / farther (comparative. 2 locations)

    Answer / teacher checkfarther
  3. Look at the listings on page 3. Chelsea Street is ___ apartment and also ___ one. (small, cheap)

    the smallest / the cheapest / smaller / cheaper / the most small / cheapest

    Answer / teacher checka

Build the sentence

Unscramble the words to make a correct sentence.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkThe marigolds are more expensive than last year
  2. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkIt is the cheapest two-bedroom apartment near the bus line

Write the correct form

Fill in the blank with the comparative or superlative form of the adjective.

  1. Of all three stores, that one has ___ (fresh) produce.
    Answer / teacher checkthe freshest
  2. This apartment is ___ (small) than the one on Bremen Street, but it is also ___ (cheap).
    Answer / teacher checksmaller, cheaper

Guide mini-quiz

  1. Rosa says: "Market Basket is cheaper than the dollar store for beans." What is she doing?

    Comparing two stores. / Saying Market Basket is the cheapest store in the city. / Saying prices at both stores are the same.

    AnswerComparing two stores.

    Comparatives (cheaper than) compare two things. Superlatives (the cheapest) rank one above all others.

  2. Rosa compares three ways to get to work. Which sentence is correct?

    The Blue Line is the most fastest. / The Blue Line is fastest. / The Blue Line is the fastest.

    AnswerThe Blue Line is the fastest.

    Superlatives need 'the' before them. Never add 'most' to an -est form.

  3. Fill in the blank: "Plan B is ___ expensive than Plan C." (Long adjective comparative: don't add -er.)
    Answermore

    Long adjectives use 'more' for comparatives. Never add -er to a long adjective like 'expensive'.

  4. Rosa compares the markets near her apartment. Put the words in order.
    AnswerThis market is the closest to my apartment

    Superlatives always need 'the' before them. 'The closest' ranks it above all others in the group.

  5. Diego says: "I want fewer problems with the landlord." Why is 'fewer' correct here?

    Because problems are uncountable. / Because problems are countable. You can count one problem, two problems. / Because 'less' only works with adjectives.

    AnswerBecause problems are countable. You can count one problem, two problems.

    'Fewer' goes with countable nouns. 'Less' goes with uncountable nouns like noise, rent, or stress.

W13: How Much / How Many: Countable + Uncountable

Weekly plan ·

Required lesson and practice

Eggs and Milk: Countable vs. Uncountable

Scene  Market Basket, Revere Beach Parkway, Thursday after work. Photo: Christiann Koepke / Unsplash

Claudette works at a hotel in East Boston. On Thursday, she stops at the store on her way home. Her sister Sarah and Sarah's big family are coming for dinner on Saturday. Claudette texts her roommate Fabienne to check what they have at home.

👩🏿
Claudette
Fabienne, do we have eggs? How many are left?
👩🏽
Fabienne
Three eggs. But we don't have milk. We need milk.
👩🏿
Claudette
OK. How much rice do we have?
👩🏽
Fabienne
Not much. Maybe half a bag.

Countable nouns are things you can count: 1 egg, 2 eggs, 3 eggs. Uncountable nouns have no plural form and no number: milk, rice, oil, money, water, bread.

Countable
an egg / three eggs a can / two cans an apple / six apples a bag / four bags
Uncountable
milk (not milks) rice (not rices) oil (not oils) money (not moneys)

Tip: Uncountable nouns are always singular. Say The rice is cheap, not The rice are cheap.

Countable or uncountable?

Choose the correct answer.

  1. Which word is uncountable?

    apples / cans / bread / bags

    Answer / teacher checkbread
  2. Which sentence is correct?

    I need three milks. / I need milk. / I need a milk.

    Answer / teacher checkb
  3. Claudette says "We need eggs." Fabienne says "We need milk." Which noun is countable?

    milk / eggs / both

    Answer / teacher checkeggs

Write your answer

Type one word.

  1. Is oil countable or uncountable?
    Answer / teacher checkuncountable

How Many or How Much?

Thursday evening, Claudette is still at the store. She has a $40 budget and twelve people are coming on Saturday, so she writes a list. Sarah, her sister, will bring the cooking oil.

Shopping list
Saturday dinner for 12 ($40)
✅ Milk: 2 bottles
✅ Eggs: 24
⬜ Rice: 1 big bag
⬜ Onions: 3

Use How many with countable nouns. Use How much with uncountable nouns.

countable How many eggs do we need?
countable How many people are coming?
uncountable How much rice do we have?
uncountable How much money do you have?

How many or how much?

Choose the correct question word.

  1. Look at the shopping list. Claudette still needs the onions. Which question is correct?

    How many onions does she need? / How much onions does she need?

    Answer / teacher checkmany
  2. Complete the question: "___ bags of rice do we need?"

    How much / How many

    Answer / teacher checkhow many
  3. Complete the question: "___ cooking oil is in the bottle?"

    How much / How many

    Answer / teacher checkhow much

Unscramble the words to make a correct question.

  1. Unscramble:
    Answer / teacher checkHow many people are coming to the party

Write your answer
